“Mine?” Petro repeated numbly, his voice sounding like it came from a dry well. “What d’you mean? This land… hasn’t it always been me farming it? My pa farmed it, my grandpappy too. It was this piece when the Germans came, and this piece when the last liberators came. How’s it become mine now?” He pointed to the familiar patch of black earth nearby, just starting to show some green shoots. “Does this stamp on this paper make the stones in the field run away by themselves? Or will next year’s rain listen to my commands?”
Old Ivan, puffing on his pipe nearby, muttered, “Careful, Petro. The Tsar used to say the land was his, then the commissar said the land was collective, now they say the land is yours. This land, eh, it’s like a disobedient wife. Nobody’s word counts, only God Almighty’s and your own strength.”
Petro ignored Ivan's grumbling. He looked down at the 'certificate' again, trying to find some familiar trace in those twisted symbols—perhaps 'potato'? Or 'tax'? Nothing. He only recognized his own name, Petro Ivanovich, clumsily printed at the top. He suddenly felt a dizzying sense of absurdity. This land, soaked with the sweat, and occasionally the blood, of generations of his family, was now 'his' because of a piece of paper he couldn't read?
He looked up at the black field, the early summer wind carrying the scent of earth and grass. The land was still the same land, silent and stoic. Slowly, carefully, he folded the stiff paper and tucked it into the worn pocket of his shirt, right next to his heart. There, the paper's edges pressed against his skin through the coarse cloth. An unprecedented emotion, a mixture of immense confusion and a tiny, almost negligible… perhaps… hope? stirred in his numb heart like a newly sprouted seedling.
Wow… he really had land? Even if only a piece of paper he couldn't make heads or tails of said so.

options.name: Well, now this mud finally has my name on it.

title: The New 'Cooperative' Neighbors
desc:
The 'land certificate' had barely warmed in Petro's breast pocket when new developments arrived in the village. This time, it wasn't an enthusiastic young man, but a stern-faced, middle-aged man who spoke with a thick bureaucratic accent. His uniform collar was stiffer than the most presentable tablecloth in Petro's house. He summoned all the villagers who had received 'certificates' and announced a grand initiative called the 'Agricultural Production Cooperative Pilot Program.'
“Comrades!” His voice echoed in the empty village hall, carrying an undeniable authority. “Individual farming is inefficient and cannot bear the heavy responsibility of revitalizing the motherland's granary! To increase output, share resources, and concentrate efforts on major tasks, we have decided to establish agricultural cooperatives! Everyone's land, tools, and even that lame old horse,” he pointed to old Ivan's animal tied to a tree, “will be uniformly managed by the cooperative, with distribution according to labor, more work means more reward!”
Petro stood in the crowd, scratching his scalp vigorously, trying to make sense of the tongue-twisting words. Uniform management? Distribution according to labor? This sounded… awfully familiar. He remembered as a child, another group of men in different uniforms had said similar things, only then it was called a 'collective farm.' Then too, they talked about 'concentrating efforts.' And the result? The grain was indeed concentrated, but it all ended up on the grain requisition teams' trucks.
“What?” Old Ivan was the first to jump up, his pipe almost falling to the ground. “My old horse may be lame, but it's mine! Why should it be uniformly managed by you? I ask you, if I want to leave a couple of potatoes for my grandson, do I have to submit a report?”
The middle-aged official pushed up his glasses, his face impassive. “Comrade Ivan Stepanovich, this is for the common good. The cooperative will uniformly provide seeds, fertilizer, and coordinate plowing times. At the end ofthe year, income will be calculated based on work points, ensuring fairness and justice, and you'll also get priority access to state-supplied agricultural machinery.” He paused, his tone becoming more emphatic. “Of course, we won't force comrades who are unwilling to join. It's just that… farmers outside the cooperative, in terms of resource allocation and agricultural product procurement prices, may… experience some differences.”
A murmur of discussion rippled through the crowd. Petro looked at the land certificate in his hand, then at the patch of land that had just started to show some life, his mind a tangled mess. The 'his' land he had just received, barely warmed, was now to be 'cooperated'? Wasn't this just going back in a circle?
But then he thought, life had indeed gotten a bit better recently. The rationed flour, though unpalatable, was at least enough; the village road had been repaired, still a dirt road, but with fewer potholes; most importantly, he could sleep soundly at night. That young coordinator had even helped his son, little Vasya, get into primary school in the city…
Petro scratched his head again. He still couldn't understand the convoluted ways of these city folk. Collective farm? Cooperative? It sounded like the big bad wolf in a new disguise. But… his stomach did feel a bit fuller than before. He sighed heavily and, like the other villagers, pressed his fingerprint onto another document he couldn't understand.

options.name: Alright, a different way to play in the mud together.

title: Divided Land, Familiar Taste
desc:
Mikhail, shouldering his oft-repaired old plow, trudged through the tilled black earth. The scent of spring finally overpowered the muddy odor of melting snow, carrying a faint, elusive fragrance of grass. Unlike previous years, the land beneath his feet, according to the red-headed document posted on the wall of the village cooperative, was now 'clearly allocated' for his family to cultivate. Of course, the lion's share of the harvest still had to go to the state, but at least, nominally, they had 'their own' land, instead of relying on the heavens and the whims of cadres for their yearly allotment.
His son, little Vasya, now almost as tall as Mikhail's shoulder, was no longer the little tyke who only knew to ask, 'Is life getting better?' He awkwardly followed his father, learning to sow a high-yield potato seed, supposedly 'scientifically cultivated.' The boy's strength had grown, and he could help quite a bit, though his movements were still clumsy, scattering seeds unevenly.
“Dad,” Vasya panted, wiping sweat from his brow, “Uncle Yakov from the cooperative said if the harvest is good this year, we can get two extra bags of potatoes! Is it true?”
Mikhail straightened up,shock his aching back, and gazed at this endless stretch of his own land. “That’s what the paper says, son.” He paused, spat. “Whether we get it in hand, well, that depends on whether God—oh no, whether Comrade Lenin’s spirit in heaven blesses us, and also on whether that fat political commissar who collects the grain is in a good mood.”
Yes, there were changes. The village loudspeaker no longer blared wartime songs daily but started promoting the benefits of 'agricultural cooperation,' saying everyone was now the master of the land. The soup in the canteen was a little thicker, occasionally with a few specks of oil. A small shop had opened in town; though its shelves were mostly empty, at least there was the idea of it.
But Mikhail knew in his heart, this land was still the same land, the soil still the same soil. What to plant, how to plant it, was mostly decided from above. How much grain to hand over, how much to keep, were iron-clad regulations. The so-called 'reward for labor' was more like the few potatoes he used to secretly pocket, now allowed to be pocketed openly—provided, of course, you first completed your delivery quota.
He watched his son scatter seeds with an excitement, an almost faith-like fervor, and his heart was a mix of emotions. Perhaps for the young, this was hope? A tangible, visible hope, even if it was only a thin layer. Well, having hope was better than having none.
Mikhail gripped the plow handles again and shouted, “Put your back into it, boy! We have to finish this furrow before dark! Otherwise, there’ll be no potato pancakes for you at dinner!”

options.name: Potato pancakes are better than no pancakes.

title: Smoke Rings by the Dnieper
desc:
The Kyiv dusk carried a scent of steel and dust, the setting sun struggling to paint the Dnieper golden, only to be sharply fragmented by the stark silhouettes of new Russian-style apartment buildings. Oleg sat at the wobbly table in his kitchen, a half-empty, almost label-less bottle of vodka and a saucer of darkly pickled cucumbers before him. His son, seventeen-year-old Sasha, was hunched over a brand-new history textbook, its pages exuding the smell of cheap ink.
“Dad,” Sasha’s voice was hesitant, breaking the silence, “the book says… we are all an indivisible part of the great Russian nation, and past sufferings were due to separatist plots and foreign powers…” He looked up, his young face etched with confusion. “But Grandma always told me we were descendants of Cossacks, singing songs of Kyivan Rus…”
Oleg didn’t answer immediately, just poured himself a full glass of vodka and downed it, a satisfied yet bitter gurgle sounding in his throat. He rolled a coarse makhorka cigarette, lit it with a match, and took a deep drag, the smoke blurring his weather-beaten face. “Books,” he finally spoke, his voice hoarse, “books are written by victors, Sasha. Like bread distributed from the ration station—they give you what they give, and you eat it, whether it tastes like sawdust mixed with mud or not.”
“But the teacher said national unity is the top priority, to forget past unpleasantness to build a strong new motherland…”
“Build a motherland?” Oleg scoffed, ash falling onto his patched trousers. “We’ve been building motherlands all our lives. First, building for some mustachioed madman in the Polish mud, then ‘building’ for those waving tridents and shouting slogans in the ruins of Crimea, then later building for some big-bearded general in the rubble of Kharkiv… Now, we’re to build for the comrades from Moscow. Every construction means tearing down something old, forgetting some old names. They say it’s for unity, for strength.” He gestured out the window. “Look at that new Comrade Street. It used to be called Khreshchatyk. Your grandma used to take me there to buy Easter eggs. Now, there are only grey concrete slabs and uniform slogans.”
Sasha fell silent, his fingers unconsciously stroking the portrait of a leader he’d never seen, printed on the book’s page. “Then… what… what are we?” the boy asked softly, a question that seemed to have troubled him for a long time.
Oleg stubbed out his cigarette and lit another. He didn’t look at Sasha but gazed at the murky waters of the Dnieper. “What are we?” he repeated, his voice dropping. “We are people who plant potatoes, who drink vodka to keep warm, who secretly sing the songs of our ancestors in our hearts. We are people who remember Khreshchatyk Street. We are people who have watched flags change again and again, yet still survive on this black earth.”
He turned, his gaze fixing on his son, sharp as a tack. “Listen, Sasha,” he said, tapping his own chest with a rough finger, then pointing to Sasha, “the blood in your veins comes from this land. The first words you spoke were in the Kyiv accent. Never, ever forget that. Even if the whole world forgets, you yourself cannot forget. You are Ukrainian.”
The father and son remained silent for a long time. Outside, the sky had completely darkened, only scattered lights twinkling on the far bank of the Dnieper. Oleg picked up the cigarette pack from the table and offered one to Sasha. Sasha hesitated, then took it. Two crimson embers glowed in the dim kitchen, smoke curling, filling the silence.

options.name: The waters of the Dnieper still flow to the Black Sea.

title: Katyusha and Quotas
desc:
When Sasha returned from school, he saw a new, almost garishly colored poster pasted at the alley entrance. It depicted a buxom, robust Ukrainian mother with a standard smile, cradling three equally rosy-cheeked infants, against a backdrop of rolling wheat fields and towering factory chimneys. A huge slogan in bold Cyrillic letters read: “Hero Mothers—The Pride and Future of the Motherland!” Smaller text detailed the latest reward policy for families with three or more children—some extra cloth coupons, and perhaps priority in purchasing low-quality candies.
At dinner, the kitchen was filled with the bland smell of boiled cabbage. Sasha, absentmindedly poking at the potato chunks in his bowl, finally spoke up: “Dad, they put up new posters in the street, saying it’s glorious to have many children, that it’s a contribution to the country… The teacher also said we have too few people, the Germans, the Americans, they have many…”
Oleg, struggling to cut a hard loaf of black bread with a dull knife, paused. He picked up the half-empty vodka bottle from the table and poured himself another glass, the murky liquid sloshing. “Glorious,” he snorted, gulping down the alcohol. “Yes, glorious. As glorious as the collective farm tractors back then. They need manpower, Sasha. They need workers to fill the factories, soldiers to fill the barracks, enough people to shout ‘Hurrah!’ and wave flags.”
He twisted a cigarette butt between his fingers. “Your grandmother’s generation, she had seven, three survived. No one called it glorious then, only hard-fated, said they couldn’t raise them. Now they want your mother, want Marsha from next door, to pop out babies like chicks from eggs. Glorious? Those cloth coupons they give, are they enough to make diapers for a newborn? Enough to buy a sip of milk? They draw you a big pie flying in the sky and then make you chase it on an empty stomach.”
Oleg lit his cigarette, took a deep drag, smoke curling. “They say we’re not the womb of Europe. Sounds nice. But they want women to open their wombs, one after another, how is that different from a sow farrowing? Marsha is only in her early thirties, looks older than your grandmother. Her man? Died two years ago in a ‘peacekeeping mission,’ on some godforsaken border, couldn’t even find his bones. Now she’s raising five kids alone, by washing clothes for officers in exchange for some potatoes. Glorious? Bullshit glorious.”
He flicked his ash. “The country needs a future, Sasha. But a future isn’t born from quotas and slogans. It’s nurtured by hot soup, by warm boots, by being able to sleep soundly at night. Don’t believe those posters, kid. The wheat in the posters can’t be eaten, the children in the posters don’t cry.”
Sasha fell silent, looking down at the few lonely potatoes in his bowl. Outside the kitchen window, the night grew darker, and the distant factory chimneys continued to spew black smoke tirelessly into the boundless twilight.

options.name: Children are the flowers of the future, but they need fertilizer, not quotas.

title: Golden Ears in Black Earth
desc:
It was time again to sell grain to the state. Oleg stood by the dusty threshing floor, watching sack after sack of plump wheat being loaded onto creaking trucks. Under the sun, the golden ears of wheat piled up like mountains, dazzling the eyes. On the radio, a broadcaster with a sonorous, perfectly enunciated voice, was passionately announcing: “…Ukraine, the granary of our great motherland, has once again over-fulfilled its aid mission to the fraternal European nations! The fertile black earth has once again proven the superiority of the system! Golden waves of wheat will nourish the entire progressive world…”
Sasha was also nearby, helping to carry sacks, sweat soaking his thin shirt. He stopped to catch his breath, wiped the sweat and dust from his face, and walked over to his father. “Dad, we’ve harvested so much grain, we really are the ‘granary of Europe’!” His young face bore a trace of pride, similar to the broadcaster’s, infected by the grand narrative.
Oleg spat out the blade of grass he was chewing, his eyes complex as he watched the departing trucks laden with grain. “Yes, a granary. Someone else’s granary.” He pulled a crumpled cigarette pack from his pocket, took one out, and lit it. “Look at this wheat, Sasha, golden and beautiful. Know where it’s going? To Moscow, to Warsaw, to Prague, to Berlin—God knows where else. It’ll become decent white bread for those city folks, a garnish on their tables.”
“But we’re helping fraternal nations, Dad. The book says this is internationalism…”
“Internationalism?” Oleg let out a dry laugh, smoke escaping from between his teeth. “Yes, great internationalism. It means tightening your belt, taking the life-sustaining grain you dug out of your fields, and loading it onto trains for ‘brothers’ thousands of versts away, whose names you don’t even know. Then they give you a few certificates, call you a ‘labor model,’ and give you a few empty promises, saying tractors will arrive in the village next year—year after year.”
He pointed to their meager private plot. “What about our own land? After handing over the public grain each year, what’s left is barely enough to get us through to spring. Your mother still has to find ways to mix potatoes with flour to make bread. We are a granary? Ha! We are sacks for others to fill with grain; once filled, they’re carried away. Who cares if the sack is torn, or if it’s hungry?”
Oleg took a harsh drag from his cigarette. “Remember, Sasha, this black earth is our mother; it can feed us. But now, it has to feed others first. When it can feed us first, before ‘aiding fraternal nations,’ then that will be truly good times. Don’t be fooled by the slogans on the loudspeakers and the numbers in the newspapers.”
The trucks kicked up a cloud of dust and drove off, leaving behind an empty threshing floor and the fragrance of wheat straw. Father and son stood there silently, watching the convoy disappear over the horizon. Oleg threw his cigarette butt to the ground, crushed it with his boot, and pulled out another from his pocket, lighting it anew.

options.name: Toiling the earth, feeding the world, starving ourselves.

title: Dust and Echoes on the Great Dam
desc:
Zaporizhzhia, on the banks of the Dnieper. Taras's sweat dripped onto the scorching concrete, evaporating instantly. The deafening roar—concrete mixers, pile drivers, the howl of heavy trucks—had almost become part of his life. He couldn't remember how many years it had been; like ants, they toiled on this war-ravaged land, rebuilding the massive hydroelectric power station that was once the pride of the republic, later a victim of both sides' scorched-earth policies.
New flags fluttered over the construction site, and loudspeakers blared perpetually optimistic marches and speeches by leading comrades about 'electrification illuminating the future.' Taras was already numb to it. He remembered earlier times, as a child, when his father had also worked here. Then, people's eyes shone with light, believing every stone, every bag of cement, was adding to a brighter world. Later, that light was extinguished, accompanied by deafening explosions and the Dnieper's angry roar. His father didn't live to see that day.
Now, they were back. With the same tenacious spirit, using equipment transported from 'fraternal republics' that often broke down, and with tens of thousands of rough hands like his own. The radio said this was a 'miracle of the people's will,' a 'powerful counterattack against fascist saboteurs.' Taras felt it was more like a struggle against themselves, against this unruly river, against that damned, ever-present past.
He and his fellow workers lived in temporary sheds, lit at night by dim bulbs—if they were lucky and the power was on. Watching the dam rise again day by day, like a grey scar across the river, Taras felt a strange emptiness. Where would this immense power flow? To light up Kyiv's neon nights, or to drive the gears of factories in distant borderlands? Perhaps both. But right now, he only felt the ache in his back, and the concrete dust that could never be completely washed away.

options.name: The river will always flow, no matter where.

title: Distant Bright Lights and Flickering Candles
desc:
On the outskirts of Poltava, Oksana once again skillfully tightened the base of a loose lightbulb. The dim yellow light flickered a few times and finally stabilized, barely illuminating her simple hut and the mending work spread out on the table. Outside, massive high-voltage power towers stood like steel giants, silently striding across the fields, extending thick cables towards a hazy distance—supposedly Poland, perhaps even further.
The radio was broadcasting the evening news, the announcer declaring in that distinctive, proud tone: “…This quarter’s electricity export quota has once again been over-fulfilled! Ukraine’s surging power is continuously being supplied to fraternal nations, strongly supporting the common prosperity of the Collective Security Treaty Organization…” Oksana snorted, paying no attention. She was more concerned about whether her electricity bill would go up again this month, and whether the village sawmill could operate normally tomorrow—the last power outage halted wood processing for half the village, leaving the men to grumble in the tavern.
Her neighbor, old Ivan, leaning on his cane, came in to borrow some salt. “Did you hear, Oksana? All our electricity is going abroad; Moscow must be very bright!” A hint of sarcasm touched the old man’s wizened face. “And here? Hah, our lightbulbs are like fireflies, on and off. Truly, the fat flows to outsiders’ fields.”
Oksana handed him the salt cellar and sighed: “Uncle Ivan, say less. They say this is the bigger picture, a ‘strategic necessity.’ What do we common folk understand?” But in her heart, she thought of her child doing homework at night, having to huddle under the lightbulb, unable to see the book clearly from a little further away. And those power lines, supposedly carrying “surging power,” hummed overhead, sending light to people she would never meet. This must be what it felt like to be a granary, she mused. Empty stomach, watching the grain being shipped away, and now even the light had to be shared with others.
She fiddled with the mending thread, by that unstable light. The distant power towers were silent silhouettes in the night, steadfastly fulfilling their 'internationalist duty'.

options.name: Currents know no borders, but darkness does.

title: Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant
desc:
Levko stood a few hundred meters away from the massive concrete dome, feeling the ground beneath his feet vibrate slightly. The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, the republic's newest pride, or rather, its newest behemoth, was undergoing some critical tests. He was a young technician, transferred from Lviv, responsible for monitoring the pressure readings of the cooling system. Everything here exuded a sense of the future, and also a chilling unfamiliarity.
The site was teeming with people in white or grey uniforms, wearing badges with numbers and letters, their faces stern. Armed guards were stationed every few steps, and the barbed wire fences bore yellow and black radiation warning signs—that strange trefoil symbol, said to represent an invisible, intangible 'fire' that could kill you. Old workers privately called it the 'atomic will-o'-the-wisp.'
Levko had received training, knew all the safety procedures, and understood what the Geiger counter readings meant. But he still couldn't completely shake off a sense of awe and a tinge of fear. This was entirely different from burning coal or damming a river. What they were taming was the power of the sun's core, the secret of stellar combustion. Propaganda posters depicted atomic energy as a gentle giant, capable of providing 'inexhaustible clean energy,' able to 'illuminate the entire republic overnight.'
However, what was locked behind those clean control rooms and thick lead doors? Levko sometimes found himself staring at the silent, immense silhouette of the reactor during night shifts. It resembled a slumbering beast, its breathing steady, but you knew it could awaken at any moment and unleash devastating power. His colleagues sometimes joked that if they made an operational error, they would instantly become 'ashes of the state.' Behind the jokes lay an unspoken tension.
Today's test seemed to be going smoothly; all readings were within normal ranges. Levko signed his name in the logbook, relieved. After work, he walked out of the plant area and saw the Dnieper River glistening in the sunset, smoke curling from a village炊 on the riverbank. Everything was peaceful and serene, as if this concrete and steel giant belonged to a different world. He didn't know what this 'peaceful atom' would ultimately bring to this land. The promised light, or a hidden shadow?
He pulled a crumpled cigarette pack from his pocket, lit one, and took a deep drag. The smell of tobacco temporarily overpowered the faint, disinfectant-like 'scientific' scent in the air.

options.name: At least the reactor didn't sneeze tonight.

title: The Dnieper's Embrace
desc:
Kyiv's night, for the first time, had a comforting, continuous expanse of lights. Along Khreshchatyk Street, twenty-year-old Yuri walked slowly. He had just finished his shift at the reconstruction site; though his body ached and the few rubles in his pocket jingled, his heart felt a strange, unprecedented sense of solidity.
He remembered his childhood, when the nights here belonged to silence, curfews, and fear. Windows had to be covered with thick black cloth; any sliver of light could attract patrols, or worse. Streetlights either didn't work or emitted a ghostly glow, making familiar streets seem alien. People spoke in hushed tones, their eyes filled with suspicion and weariness.
Later, flags changed again and again, each time accompanied by new slogans, new promises, and new destruction and displacement. Yuri's father, a taciturn railway worker, never showed enthusiasm for any flag or any 'liberator,' merely quietly repairing bombed-out tracks, only to see them bombed again. Father often said: “It doesn't matter what sign they hang, Yuri, our life is just mending pots; one hole is plugged, another leaks.”
But now, something seemed genuinely different. The roadside cafes were lit with warm lights, and low conversations and the long-absent sound of a bandura drifted out. A few students in new, albeit drab but clean, school uniforms were gathered, laughing and discussing something, no longer whispering. Even the old beggar at the street corner had a few more coins in his can today.
Yuri walked to the Dnieper, leaning on the half-repaired granite railing. The river flowed silently in the night, the lights from the opposite bank reflecting on the water, shattered into a million golden scales. The air was filled with the river's dampness and the scent of freshly turned earth, free of the smell of gunpowder and the pervasive iron tang of fear that had lingered for years.
He remembered his grandmother's dying words, when he was just a child and didn't quite understand. Grandma held his hand, her cloudy eyes gazing at the ceiling, whispering in her thick Ukrainian accent: “Yurik, child… home, is home… no matter how many times it’s trampled, how many bowls are broken… as long as the roots are in the soil, it will always… grow back…”
A girl in similar work clothes, her face equally tired but with a different kind of radiance, walked past him carrying a basket. Seeing him, she smiled a little shyly and quickened her pace. Yuri watched her figure disappear at the end of the dim streetlight.
He suddenly understood his grandmother's words. This land, this city, these people speaking with the same Kyiv accent as him—no matter how much suffering they had endured, no matter how many identities had been imposed upon them—this was home. Now, it seemed someone had finally remembered to sweep the courtyard, mend the roof, and make this home feel like a home again.
The road to reconstruction was long and arduous; his father's skepticism might still hold true. But tonight, standing by this timeless river, watching that awakening expanse of their lights, Yuri felt for the first time, truly, that they weren't just patching a hole, but re-embracing a scarred, yet finally warming, home. This was their time, a time to rediscover themselves.
He pulled the last crumpled cigarette from his pocket, hesitated, then put it back. Perhaps, he thought, it was time to quit some old habits too.

options.name: This time, the river embraces both banks.

title: Bayan Music and Mutton Soup in the Barracks
desc:
Night fell, and in a workers' barracks at a large reconstruction site on the outskirts of Moscow, the dim glow of a kerosene lamp barely dispelled the shadows in the corners, yet it couldn't drive away the pervasive smell of sweat, tobacco, and some rich food. In the center of the barracks, on a makeshift table cobbled together from several wooden crates, sat a large, steaming iron pot. Inside, potatoes and a few precious pieces of mutton tumbled, the source of the rich aroma.
Four men of different complexions and accents sat around it, their faces etched with the day's fatigue, yet radiating a rare sense of relaxation.
“Ivan, your skill is still unmatched, these potatoes are melting in my mouth!” said Rustam, a Tatar man, praising Ivan indistinctly as he chewed on a potato, a thumbs-up gesture punctuating his words.
Ivan, a typical robust Russian, grinned, revealing a few teeth yellowed by smoke. “Of course, look who cooked it! But Rustam, this mutton is your credit. If it weren't for your connections, getting this good stuff from our ‘Southern comrades,’ we’d be eat dry bread and cold water tonight.”
“Hey, this is called resource integration, understand? Taras here got us good firewood, Giorgi exchanged for salt… We all chip in, that’s how we get by.” Rustam patted his chest, then pointed to the quietly smiling Ukrainian lad Taras, and to Giorgi, a Georgian, who was carefully carving something with a small knife.
Taras smiled shyly and picked up the old bayan accordion beside him, testing a few notes. “So… shall I play a tune? To liven things up?”
“Play! You must play!” Ivan waved his hand grandly. “Play ‘Katyusha,’ but make it cheerful, don’t play it like a funeral dirge!”
Melodious notes filled the air. Though the accordion was somewhat out of tune and the player’s skill was far from exquisite, in this humble barracks, it sounded exceptionally moving. Giorgi stopped his work—he was carving a pair of small wooden figures, seemingly a couple dancing the Lezginka. He picked up a coarse earthenware bowl, filled it with mutton soup, and then filled bowls for the others one by one.
“To…” Giorgi raised his bowl, his deep-set eyes twinkling in the lamplight. “To us still being able to sit together and drink soup, to this damned war finally being over, to us still being able to rebuild this land with our own hands… no matter where we come from.”
“To being alive!” Ivan roared, clinking his bowl first.
“To peace!” Rustam followed suit.
“To home…” Taras said softly, the music never stopping.
Four rough bowls clinked together with a dull thud, mingling with the melody of the bayan and the gurgling of the mutton soup in the pot. They came from different corners, spoke different dialects, worshipped different gods, and in chaotic times, had even suspected or fought each other. But now, on this ravaged yet revitalizing land, before a pot of hot mutton soup and an out-of-tune song, they were first and foremost workmates, brothers, people who moved bricks together for tomorrow. The road to reconstruction was long, longer than the Volga, but at least tonight, they had hot soup, music, and each other.

options.name: Down this hot soup, and tomorrow we continue!

title: Tides and Ink
desc:
The air in Riga's port was thick with the smell of sea salt, diesel, and an inescapable dust of the past. Antonov, a young planner dispatched from Moscow, stood in the biting sea breeze, trying to pin a huge blueprint titled “Baltic Coast Reconstruction Zone – Phase One” onto several rusty oil drums. The wind was uncooperative, and a corner of the blueprint flapped noisily, like a flag unwilling to surrender.
Nearby, several Latvian dockworkers silently moved bags of cement unloaded from a cargo ship that looked as old as Antonov's grandfather. Their gazes passed over Antonov and his blueprint, out towards the grey Baltic Sea, their expressions complex and indecipherable, like the unpredictable weather of this region.
Antonov knew how magnificent this plan was—new quays, modernized warehouses, efficient railway connections… The lines on the blueprint were neat, precise, filled with a rational beauty. But the reality was: the quays were pockmarked with war craters, warehouse roofs had either collapsed or were mere skeletons, and the only thing that looked reasonably sturdy was a concrete bunker built by the Germans, now a canvas for children's graffiti and a playground. The “skilled workforce” mentioned in the plan was currently communicating in a peculiar mix of Latvian, Russian, and German, and their efficiency… well, one could say it was full of improvisational artistry.
He sighed, using a stone to weigh down the unruly corner of the blueprint. This reconstruction plan was like this blueprint: beautiful, grand, but also fragile, liable to be blown detalhes by the harsh winds of reality at any moment.

options.name: Where the ink dries, reality only begins to develop.

title: Thawing Words
desc:
Tallinn, the cobblestone streets glistening with a damp chill after the rain. Irma, an old woman who had worked in a tailor shop for most of her life, was carefully climbing a creaking wooden ladder to her cluttered, almost forgotten attic. Outside, the laughter of children chasing each other mingled with the intermittent sounds of hammering from a distant construction site—these were sounds that had only recently reappeared in the city. In the past, children wouldn't laugh so loudly, and adults' footsteps were always hurried and cautious.
Forty years is long enough for fear to seep into the bones, to become an instinct. Irma remembered the men in grey uniforms, speaking harsh German, patrolling the streets; the dead silence of curfewed streets and occasional gunshots; neighbors disappearing silently, never to return; the forbidden books, forbidden songs, forbidden language whispered. Estonia's soul seemed frozen in amber, heavy and transparent.
Under an old leather suitcase in the attic, she found a small booklet wrapped in oilcloth. Unwrapping it revealed a yellowed, brittle poetry collection, its cover bearing the name of a national poet she had admired in her youth—a name no one had dared to mention publicly for decades. Her fingers trembled as she caressed the lead-printed words, the words that had sustained her through the long dark nights, the verses that sang of forests, seas, and freedom.
She sat on the dusty floor, reading silently by the dim light filtering through the small attic window. She read slowly, as if relearning each word, each syllable awakening dormant memories. She seemed to see her younger self again, reciting these poems with friends on the university lawn, the sky then seeming particularly blue, the possibilities of the future as expansive as summer clouds.
Later… later everything changed. Friends either went into exile, fell silent, or disappeared. Only this poetry collection, like a tenacious seed, had endured the long winter in the dark soil.
From downstairs came her granddaughter Lina's voice: “Grandma! Dinner's ready! What are you looking for up there?”
Irma carefully closed the poetry book, rewrapped it in oilcloth, and hid it back under the suitcase. She stood up, brushing dust from her clothes. “Nothing, child,” she called towards the staircase, her voice a little hoarse, but warmer than before, “Just found some… old things.” She descended the stairs; outside, the sky had darkened, and lights flickered on at the distant construction site. Some wounds might never fully heal, but at least, frozen words were finally beginning to thaw quietly in her heart.

options.name: Memories are like seeds, waiting for spring.

title: The Sea Heeds No Reports
desc:
Murmansk dawn, carrying a salty and biting tang. Old fisherman Stepan and his two sons were struggling to haul a heavy fishing net onto their weather-beaten trawler, the 'Victory.' In the net, silver cod and a few struggling flounders thrashed about on deck. This was their catch from an entire night's work—not abundant, but enough to give the family hope, and much better than the days of sneaking out to sea during the war, terrified of German patrol boats.

“Dad! Look at this one! It’s fat!” Youngest son Volodya excitedly held up a large, wriggling flounder, his face red from the cold, yet beaming with the joy of the catch.

Stepan nodded, spitting out the cigarette butt he was chewing. “Don’t dawdle, sort and pack them quickly. That uniformed小子 from the port authority will be here soon.” The 'uniformed小子' he referred to was the new government’s fisheries representative, a young man with glasses, who spoke in a bookish manner and always carried a folder full of numbers.

Sure enough, as soon as the boat docked, the young man appeared, followed by two rifle-carrying soldiers—a presence that made the other fishermen on the quay somewhat nervous. “Comrade Stepan Nikolayevich,” the young man pushed up his glasses and opened his folder, “According to the ‘Five-Year Plan for Sustainable Development of Northern Fisheries and Productivity Enhancement,’ your catch quota for today is… hmm… three hundred kilograms. Please cooperate with the inspection.”

Stepan glanced at the fish piled on deck, then at the form in the young man’s hand. A wry smile touched his swarthy face. “Comrade, you see, the wind was wrong today, the schools didn’t come. We worked all night and only got…”

“Regulations are regulations, Comrade Stepan.” The young man interrupted him, his tone brooks no argument, though a hint of helplessness seemed to flicker in his eyes. “The plan requires precise data. Everyone must meet their targets. This is for the state, for the overall benefit.” He pointed to the distant cold storage warehouses and processing plants under construction. “Think about it, in the future, our fish can be transported to Moscow, to even farther places! Everyone will be able to eat fish!”

Stepan didn’t argue further. He silently worked with his sons to weigh and register the catch. Three hundred kilograms was the quota; they had achieved less than half of that today. The young man meticulously recorded the numbers, made a few checkmarks in his notebook, reminded them they had to “double their efforts” tomorrow, and then left with the soldiers.

Elder son Dmitry grumbled under his breath, “Dad, what kind of nonsense is this? The sea isn’t a factory; it can’t produce fish according to a plan.”

Stepan patted his son’s shoulder, picked up a torn net, and began expertly mending it. “The sea heeds no reports, son,” he said calmly, gazing at the churning grey waves of the Barents Sea. “It only gives what it’s willing to give. As for us, we just take it, mend our nets, and go out again tomorrow.” Sunlight pierced through the clouds, falling on the patched net and on the old man’s wrinkled face, reflecting a calmness that was neither joyous nor desperate.

options.name: Tomorrow, the nets must still be cast into the sea.

title: Forest Echoes
desc:
Static crackled from the radio as Lieutenant Sergeyev stubbed out his cigarette on the damp moss. The order was brief, cold, like the late autumn rain in Latvia: “Order: Sector 7-G, execute ‘Forest Combing’ operation. Known hostile armed unit, codename ‘Fox,’ active in the area. Objective: Search and clear. Repeat, search and clear. Over.”
Here we go again. Sergeyev cursed inwardly but made no sound. The so-called 'Forest Brothers,' a fine name for a bunch of ghosts hiding in the woods. Sometimes they ambushed supply lines like real soldiers, other times they harassed villages like bandits. They knew this forest like a bear knows its den. And Sergeyev and his men, mostly greenhorns from the Volga steppes or Ural mining towns, had less sense of direction in this labyrinthine forest than a startled elk.
“Boss,” Sergeant Major Petrovich sidled up, handing him a canteen filled with watered-down spirits, “Chasing ‘Foxes’ again? That ‘Badger’ last time gave us a hell of a run, and we lost two good men.” Petrovich was a veteran, his face etched with the annals of war, his eyes holding a world-weary fatigue.
“Orders are orders, old Pet.” Sergeyev took a swig, the fiery liquid burning his throat. “The higher-ups said the Baltics must be ‘thoroughly stabilized.’ These ‘brothers’ in the woods are the last nails; they have to be pulled out.”
“Stabilized?” Petrovich scoffed. “Pull out the nails, and there are still stones in the earth. We drove out the Germans, but to them, we’re occupiers too, just with different insignia. This job… it has no end.”
Sergeyev fell silent. He knew Petrovich was right. They had won the Great Patriotic War, driven the Nazis back to their homeland, but the ghost of war seemed to linger, merely changing its face, hiding in this gloomy forest. Each 'combing' felt like fighting his own shadow—exhausting, bloody, and never knowing when a cold shot might come from some tree hollow.
“Check your gear! Move out in five!” Sergeyev shouted to his men, his voice echoing in the empty woods. “All of you, damn it, stay alert! Don’t let the forest mosquitoes suck you dry!” He tried to dispel the pervading gloom with coarse humor, but to little effect. The soldiers silently checked their weapons, their eyes vacant.
Maybe this time they’d catch that damned 'Fox,' Sergeyev thought. Maybe this time fewer men would die. Maybe… He stopped thinking, just tightened his pack straps and was the first to step into the ever-thickening depths of the forest.

options.name: Deep in the forest, only the wind answers.

title: Embers in the Wolf's Den
desc:
“Target confirmed, coordinates Delta-9, enemy strongpoint, suspected 'Werewolf' remnant nest. Requesting artillery support, repeat, requesting artillery support. Over.” Second Lieutenant Kostya reported calmly into the radio, his voice devoid of any tremor, as if he were announcing today's lunch menu. He lay prone behind the ruins of a bombed-out farmhouse, flanked by several equally calm soldiers, observing a distant, well-camouflaged bunker through binoculars.

'Werewolves'—the mess left behind by the Germans, a motley crew of diehard Nazis, local collaborators, or simply brainwashed fanatics. They weren't as elusive as the 'Forest Brothers,' but far more frenzied and cruel. Their attacks were often without warning and exceedingly vicious, leaving only scorched earth and dismembered corpses. Dealing with them involved no negotiation, no mercy, only complete 'zeroing out.'

A few minutes later, a dull roar emanated from the distant artillery positions. Seconds later, a piercing shriek approached from afar, and the earth began to tremble. Orange fireballs erupted around the bunker, sending thick smoke and dust skyward. Kostya lowered his binoculars, rubbing his ears, which were numb from the concussion.

“Fire mission complete. Alpha team, prepare to mop up. Beta team, flank cover. Maintain communications, watch for crossfire. Advance!” Kostya issued commands via his throat mic. The soldiers skillfully provided covering fire for each other, rapidly advancing towards the still-smoking target area.

The entry into the bunker was smoother than expected; resistance was minimal. The interior reeked of gunpowder, blood, and a nauseating stench of decay. Swastikas and unintelligible slogans were scrawled on the walls. In a corner, a few crates of German-made ammunition and canned food were piled next to several charred or dismembered bodies; SS collar tabs could still be faintly discerned on their tattered uniforms.

A soldier kicked open a rickety iron door. Inside, a shockingly young, blond boy cowered in a corner, clutching a MP40 with a broken stock. Seeing the soldiers rush in, he let out an inhuman scream and tried to raise the useless weapon.

“Target neutralized,” an old soldier’s voice sounded, accompanied by a crisp gunshot.

Kostya didn’t go in to look. He just stood at the entrance for a moment, listening to the sounds of searching and clearing from within. “Report to HQ, 'Siren' nest has been cleared, conducting battlefield assessment. Over.” He picked up the radio again, his voice still calm. The war was over, but cleaning up the garbage it left behind felt like an endless chore. He felt an inexplicable weariness, more profound than after a three-day forced march.

options.name: Beneath the ashes, embers always remain.

title: Familiar Strangers at the Street Corner
desc:
Anna Petrovna, carrying a tray of freshly baked rye bread, stood somewhat hesitantly at her neighbor's door. She had lived in this apartment building in Vilnius's Old Town for nearly thirty years. Neighbors had come and gone: pre-war Lithuanians, Soviet-era Russian cadres, German officers' families during the occupation... Now, a new Russian family had moved in; the husband was said to be an engineer transferred from Siberia.
The stairwell smelled of familiar borscht, mixed with the scent of newly painted walls. Anna took a deep breath and knocked. A woman her own age opened the door, her face etched with the weariness of a long journey and a hint of不易察觉 nervousness. “Hello,” Anna said in somewhat rusty but still fluent Russian, “I'm Anna, from next door. Welcome to the neighborhood. This is freshly baked bread, please try some.”
The hostess was momentarily愣住, then a grateful smile spread across her face. “Oh, thank you so much, Anna Petrovna! Please come in, come in! I'm Natasha, and this is my husband, Ivan.” A middle-aged man, similarly weathered by hardship, emerged from inside, awkwardly wiping oil stains from his hands.
The room was simple, sparsely furnished, but tidily kept. A brand-new map hung on the wall, with several place names circled in red: Moscow, Leningrad, and Omsk, the city they had just left. “You must have had a tiring journey,” Anna said, placing the bread on the table, “Coming from so far away.”
“Yes,” Ivan sighed. “We packed up and left as soon as we got the transfer orders. They said engineers were needed here, for… for reconstruction.” He looked out the window at the familiar church spires and the slightly unfamiliar streets. “Vilnius is a good place, it’s just… a bit different.”
Anna understood what he meant. For old residents like her, the city changed its face under different flags, each time meaning a redefinition of identity. And for ‘newcomers’ like Ivan and Natasha, they were both builders sent by the victors and strangers needing to put down new roots in this land. Russian was being taught in schools again, street signs had been changed, and newspapers daily propagandized the “great Russian family of nations” and “brotherly friendship.” Yet the Lithuanian old lady selling flowers downstairs looked at her much the same way she had looked at the German occupiers.
“It will be alright,” Anna said softly, unsure if she was comforting her new neighbors or herself. “Slowly, everyone has to learn to live again.”
Natasha poured her a cup of hot tea. “I hope so,” she said in a low voice. “The children really like the park here.”
Perhaps that was where hope lay, Anna thought. Children’s worlds were always simpler. Maybe their generation could truly find a new identity on this ancient land, one belonging to Russians and to everyone, unburdened by the heavy baggage of the past.

options.name: Time either dilutes everything or deepens the scars.

title: Leaflets in the Wind
desc:
Maris, a tram conductor in Riga, was listlessly watching the familiar streetscape outside his window. A light rain had just fallen, freshening the air, and the leaves of the chestnut trees lining the street were a vibrant green. The tram clanged past Freedom Monument Square—the statue symbolizing Latvian independence, which, after being defaced and restored under various regimes, now stood in its original form again, albeit with a few indelible scars on its base.
This morning, new propaganda posters had appeared all over the city. Their style was bright, their colors vivid, a stark contrast to the gloomy, oppressive German posters or the stiff, formulaic Soviet slogans of the past. One poster depicted a blonde girl and a dark-haired boy holding hands, running through a sunlit wheat field, with the new Russian flag and the Kremlin's spires in the background. Another showed workers and peasants (their attire quite local in character) smiling broadly, holding hammers, sickles, and gears, with the slogan: “You are a citizen of a free country! Let us build a prosperous homeland together!”
The tram reached a stop, and several workers, just off their shift, boarded. They grumbled about new factory regulations while quietly discussing the new posters. “Freedom? Whose freedom?” an older worker muttered. “The Germans left, the Russians came again. Same soup, different bowl.”
“But it’s different this time, isn’t it?” a younger one countered. “I hear we’ll be able to elect our own mayor, and the newspapers can even criticize bureaucrats a bit.”
“Sounds good,” the old man shook his head. “Let’s see when it actually happens. Freedom, that’s not something you get just by pasting up a few pictures.”
Maris listened silently, not interjecting. He had experienced too many ‘liberations.’ The Soviets came, saying they were liberating them from the bourgeoisie. The Germans came, saying they were liberating them from the Bolsheviks. Now, new Russians had come, saying they were “citizens of a free country.” What color was freedom, really? Was it the bright, vivid color of the posters, or was it like his own faded, washed-out old uniform—grey, and tinged with an unspoken weariness?
A gust of wind blew, and a few leaflets, from who knows where, landed on the tram tracks. They bore slogans similar to the posters, along with some clauses about new civic rights and duties. Maris watched them get run over by the wheels, turning into a blurred pulp. Perhaps, this time it really was different? Perhaps freedom wasn't just a color, but the right, after everything, to show even a little bit of green, like the chestnut leaves outside his window now? He didn't know. He could only, as usual, pull the cord to signal departure and continue his daily routine.

options.name: The sky before dawn is always the most confusing.

title: Preliminary Assessment Report on the Industrial Status of the Baltic Coastal Region
desc:
To: Responsible Comrades, Baltic Coastal Provisional Administrative Committee
From: Kovalev, Section Two, Regional Economic Development Department, Central Planning Bureau
Subject: Preliminary Assessment of Industrial Potential in Your Region and Subsequent Work Directives
Comrades,

The preliminary assessment report on the industrial facilities in your region has been received. After initial study by our bureau, the relevant spirit is conveyed as follows:

The assessment team's report indicates that the region possesses certain industrial potential, particularly in port transshipment and some heavy industries left behind or modified by the Germans. This is largely consistent with the Central Committee's expectations. However, it must be clearly recognized that severe war damage, outdated technology, labor shortages, and chaotic standards are also prominent issues. These are serious obstacles hindering the region's integration into the overall national economic plan. Overcoming these obstacles is your committee's current overriding task.

The Central Committee expects you to, with a high degree of revolutionary enthusiasm and a pragmatic attitude, immediately begin repairing key infrastructure (especially the ports of Riga, Tallinn, Klaipėda, and railway lines), rectifying the labor force and submitting skill assessment data, and standardizing production, to lay a solid foundation for subsequent larger-scale investment and construction. Regarding specific investment directions and resource allocation, the Central Committee will make unified arrangements based on the detailed plan you submit next and the overall national needs.

Do not wait or rely on others; take a proactive stance. Subsequent instructions will be issued separately.

options.name: For the great reconstruction. Central Planning Bureau, Kovalev

title: Gears and Amber
desc:
The former 'Radiotehnika' factory, once the pride of Riga, had transformed into a larger, noisier, and somehow… stranger behemoth. The vast workshops were expanded, swallowing several nearby alleys and a defunct amber workshop. Towering chimneys tirelessly belched thick smoke, dyeing the sky an industrial grey. On the assembly lines, conveyor belts ran ceaselessly, emitting a monotonous, deafening hum. The air reeked of machine oil, solder, and sweat.

Aldis, an old artisan who had crafted amber jewelry for generations, was now an assembly worker on one of these lines. His once nimble fingers, capable of polishing a rough piece of amber into a translucent work of art, now fumbled to press standardized plastic knobs into equally standardized radio casings. The movements were repetitive, mechanical, as if he himself had become part of the machine.

“Hurry up, Aldis! Don’t fiddle around like a sissy!” the foreman bellowed, a burly Russian with a thick accent. “This batch is due in Voronezh this afternoon! If we don’t meet the quota, nobody gets a bonus!”

Aldis sighed and quickened his pace. He didn’t miss the past; under German rule, his small workshop had long since closed. Survival was enough. Now, at least, there was work, a fixed ration of black bread, and occasional dried fish. But as he looked at the identical radio casings on the assembly line, he always felt something was missing. The amber pieces he once meticulously carved, each with its unique pattern and luster, were like individual souls. Now, everything was standardized, centralized, for efficiency, for that grand 'Plan.'

During his lunch break, he secretly took out a small piece of unsubmitted rough amber from his pocket, gently caressing its warm surface with his fingertips. Sunlight, filtering through the grimy window, seemed to ignite a tiny golden spark within the small piece of amber, a remnant of a bygone era.

options.name: A gear might turn the world, but it cannot polish the soul's luster.

title: Red Lines on the Sea Chart
desc:
The 'Victory' dropped anchor fifteen nautical miles offshore. Captain Stepan spat out his cigarette butt and squinted at the horizon. The weather was good today; seagulls circled overhead, a sign of possible fish schools. But his brow was furrowed.
“Dad, we can’t go any further west,” elder son Dmitry said, pointing to a brand-new sea chart with red dashed lines. “Look, this is the new boundary of the ‘Third Fishing Zone.’ Any further and we’re in the Second Zone, and we don’t have a permit for that.”
Stepan snorted but said nothing. He had fished these waters his whole life. When did he ever need someone to tell him with red lines where the fish were and where they weren’t? Fish don’t read maps! But now, everything had changed. New regulations, new zonal demarcations, and those inspectors in their brand-new patrol boats, dressed in crisp uniforms, constantly scribbling in their notebooks. They said it was for “scientific management,” “sustainable development,” for the “national interest.”
“But old Jonas said yesterday there were fish aplenty in the Second Zone, like rain!” younger son Volodya chimed in. “They hauled in a full net yesterday!”
“Shut up, Volodya!” Dmitry glared at him. “Do you want the inspectors to impound our boat? Old Anders’ boat crossed the line just a little last time and got fined a hefty sum!”
Stepan sighed and picked up his binoculars, fruitlessly scanning the grey expanse of the sea. The sea was still the same sea, churning for decades, merciless and generous. Only now, there were many invisible lines on its surface, and visible grey patrol boats crisscrossing. He didn’t know if these red lines and forms would increase the catch, but he knew freedom had diminished. He waved his hand: “Haul in the nets. Let’s see what luck we have today.” The nets were slowly winched up, containing only a few small fish and a mass of slimy seaweed.

options.name: The sea remains silent, but the rules ashore have multiplied.

title: Sighs in the Canteen
desc:
Thursday, 'Weekly Fish Day' again. The communal canteen of Tallinn's Twelfth Textile Factory reeked of a strong, indescribable fishy smell, mixed with the bland aroma of boiled potatoes. Canteen cook Ilena was listlessly stirring a large pot of murky, viscous 'fish soup' with a huge ladle, in which floated a few suspicious white fish chunks and grey potato pieces.

“Aunt Ilena, could the fish soup today… er… have a bit more salt?” a young female worker asked cautiously, holding her tray.
Ilena, her face smudged with grease and sweat, managed a wry smile. “Silly girl, salt is also rationed according to the plan! Besides, no matter how much salt you add, this fish will taste the same.” She was referring to the mountains of frozen cod blocks piled in the warehouse—supposedly “the fruits of over-fulfilled tasks by comrades in the Northern Fisheries Zone.” Fresh they were, but that persistent sea-fish smell, no amount of cooking could get rid of it.

A propaganda poster hung on the wall, depicting a beaming chef (in a chef’s uniform a hundred times cleaner than Ilena’s) holding a platter of seemingly golden-crisp fried fish garnished with lemon slices. The slogan beside it read: “Fish is nutritious, aiding national construction!” Workers queued silently, taking their portions of the fish soup and black bread, which bore no resemblance to the poster. Some were expressionless, some frowned, and others tried to hide the fish chunks with their black bread, drinking only the watery soup.

“Back in the day,” an old worker in the corner said softly to his companion, while blowing on his scalding fish soup, “right after the war, having anything to eat was good enough. Now, at least we get ‘meat’ weekly, even if it’s fish…” He paused, prodding a piece of mushy fish in his bowl with his spoon. “Just don’t know if this fish came from the Baltic Sea, or from some planning committee’s head.” This drew a suppressed chuckle from his companion. Ilena heard it, merely shook her head, and continued stirring the large pot of fish soup, which carried both the national plan and the workers’ stomach acid.

options.name: The plan fills the stomach, but not the palate.

title: Seaside Sanatorium
desc:
Jūrmala beach, fine sand, green pine forests, a cool sea breeze. Valentin, a model tractor driver from Ryazan Oblast, stood somewhat awkwardly by the sea in brand-new, ill-fitting beach shorts. It was his first time seeing the sea, and his first time receiving a unit-awarded “Ten-Day Trip to the Baltic Seaside Sanatorium.” The brochure said it was a “workers’ paradise, a haven for physical and mental relaxation.”

The sanatorium itself was an imposing building in the Soviet neoclassical style, formerly a holiday villa for high-ranking German officers, it was said. The rooms were clean and tidy, and the food was much better than the factory canteen. Mornings were scheduled with gymnastics and “health lectures,” and afternoons could be spent strolling by the sea or participating in organized volleyball matches. Everything was orderly, filled with “organized care.”

Only… Valentin always felt something was amiss. Apart from them—the “advanced workers” from various places and their families—there were hardly any locals on the beach. Occasionally, a few Latvian children played in the distance, eyeing this group of “tourists” in uniform sanatorium attire with a mixture of curiosity and detachment. The shops had few goods, yet prices were not cheap, and the shopkeepers’ attitudes were hardly enthusiastic. Traces of hastily painted-over German slogans could still be seen on the sanatorium walls.

At night, he drank home-brought vodka with Ivan, a miner from Kursk, who shared his room. “Old Ivan,” Valentin said, looking out at the dark sea, “do you think this place is really as good as the posters say? I always feel… it’s a bit desolate.”

Ivan, after a drunken burp, exhaled a smoke ring. “Good or not, isn’t it all a state benefit? Free food and lodging, and we get to see the sea. Much better than being down in the mines. As for desolate…哼, the Germans only left a few years ago, it’s good enough that it’s recovered this much. Wait a few years, when we’ve completely rebuilt it, then it’ll be a real paradise!” He clapped Valentin firmly on the shoulder. “Don’t think so much, come, drink! To health! To the motherland!”

Valentin raised his glass and clinked it with Ivan’s. Perhaps Ivan was right; he should enjoy this rare holiday and not overthink. But gazing at the vast, silent Baltic Sea shimmering silver under the moonlight, he couldn’t help wondering, what was this sea like in the memories of the local people?

options.name: Footprints on the sand, of varying depths.

title: Shadows in the Black Cat Café
desc:
The cobblestone streets of Riga's Old Town had been newly repaired, and the medieval buildings lining them had their facades carefully restored, adorned with fresh bilingual street signs in Russian and Latvian. In the newly opened 'Black Cat Café,' under soft lighting, several young people conversed in low tones, the air filled with the aroma of coffee and a faint scent of tobacco. A few modernist paintings (approved by the cultural department) hung on the walls, and a gramophone in the corner played a melodious Soviet light music piece. Everything seemed so calm, orderly, and full of hope for a new life.

Yelena, a freshman studying history at Riga University, sat by the window with her classmate Andris. Yelena was from Moscow, full of curiosity about this ancient city imbued with exotic charm. Andris was a local; his grandfather had once been a famous lawyer in the city.

“It’s incredible, isn’t it, how quickly things have changed?” Yelena mused, stirring her coffee. “Before I came, I saw photos, and this place was all rubble.”

“Yes, they work fast,” Andris said softly, his gaze sweeping over the ‘excessively’ perfect guildhall outside the window. “It’s like magic, covering up all the old scars.”

“Isn’t that good?” Yelena asked, puzzled. “Saying goodbye to the past, welcoming the future, that’s what we should be doing.”

Andris fell silent for a moment, taking a sip of his coffee. “Perhaps. It’s just that sometimes, I feel they’re covering up more than just scars.” He lowered his voice. “Did you know? This café used to be a German security service outpost. The basement… many bad things happened there.” He pointed to an inconspicuous vent in the corner. “A friend of my grandfather, a poet, was taken from here and never came back.”

Yelena followed his gaze to the smooth wall and a brightly colored landscape painting. That cheerful Soviet music continued its tireless loop. She suddenly found the coffee a bit off-tasting. This revitalized city, like a meticulously dressed beauty, was beautiful yet carried an imperceptible chill. The erased histories, the concealed memories, had they truly vanished? Or did they, like the shadows in the basement, still lurk beneath this glamorous surface?

options.name: Beneath new paint, old marks still whisper.

title: Beach Umbrellas on the Sand
desc:
On Jūrmala beach, a few new, brightly colored beach umbrellas were sporadically set up. Beneath them sat tourists, mostly model workers from inland Russian factories and their families, dressed in unaccustomed swimwear, their skin slightly sunburned, faces alight with novelty and a touch of reserve. Seagulls circled overhead, their familiar, long calls echoing.

Anna, an old Latvian woman selling homemade amber bracelets and shell trinkets at a beach stall, silently arranged her wares as she watched the scene. These tourists were different from the German officers of wartime, and different too from the匆匆 Soviet commissars of the early days. They awkwardly learned to enjoy the sun and sea breeze, cautiously exchanged rubles for the not-so-exquisite souvenirs at her stall, and even offered thanks in broken Latvian.

The aroma of coffee wafted from the newly opened state-run café nearby, where several uniformed waiters were wiping the windows. In the distance, the clanging sounds of construction could be heard; a larger sanatorium, capable of hosting foreign friends, was supposedly being built.

“Everything is getting better, isn’t it?” the uncle selling smoked fish at the next stall whispered to Anna in Latvian. Anna nodded, looking at a little Russian girl excitedly picking up a seashell, then at the distant grey-blue Baltic Sea. Yes, at least there were umbrellas on the beach now, and the laughter of tourists, instead of barbed wire and the boot prints of patrolmen. That was enough, for now.

options.name: Under the sun, some things are quietly growing.

title: A Sailor's Dream
desc:
The port, like an awakened giant, throbbed with the clang of steel, the roar of machinery, and the resonant shanties of sailors. Sixteen-year-old Mikhail, newly arrived from an inland village to report to this sprawling base in Tallinn, stared wide-eyed. He had never seen so many ships—though most looked rust-eaten, some still in dry dock being hammered and banged, like patients awaiting some mysterious surgery. But he also saw several new, grey-painted patrol boats cruising the harbor, and in the distance, a massive gantry crane, supposedly capable of building submarines, was under construction.

“New kid, eh?” an old sailor, polishing a deck gun, grinned at his bewildered look, revealing tobacco-stained teeth. “Don’t just stand there gawking. Report to your political commissar. Be late, and you’ll get your arse kicked!”

“Yes, Comrade!” Mikhail saluted, somewhat awkwardly but with enthusiasm. “I… I came to be a sailor! I want to be on the biggest ship! To defend our coastline!”

The old sailor’s smile faded slightly. He patted Mikhail’s thin shoulder. “Good lad, got ambition. But the navy ain’t just about standing on deck admiring the view. First, learn how to polish this damned brass cannon until it reflects your silly face.” He pointed to a nearby pile of potatoes. “Or go help in the galley first, tonight’s dinner depends on you.”

Mikhail wasn’t discouraged in the least. To wear this blue-and-white striped sailor’s shirt, to breathe this air thick with sea salt and machine oil, to see these steel behemoths representing national power—he was already content. He imagined himself standing on a mighty warship, riding the waves, sending any daring enemy to the bottom of the sea. Yes, that was his dream! Even if it started with peeling potatoes, he would set sail!

options.name: The sea is calling, in the name of steel and steam.

title: Conversation on a Park Bench
desc:
The evening glow gilded the park next to Riga's Freedom Square with a warm golden hue. Two figures, a man and a woman, no longer young, sat side by side on a bench, silently watching children chase each other by the fountain, their laughter like silver bells. New streetlights had come on, illuminating the freshly paved paths and neatly trimmed flowerbeds. The clanging of a passing tram and faint radio music from a distant window drifted through the air.

“Big changes, aren't there?” he spoke first, his voice somewhat hoarse, like an old, unused bellows. “Remember what it used to be like here? Curfews, patrols, and…” He paused, not continuing.

“I remember,” she said softly, her gaze fixed on the tall Freedom Monument in the center of the square, its surface showing faint traces of repair. “Back then, the sky was always grey, even children didn't dare laugh out loud.” She pulled her scarf tighter, though the weather wasn't particularly cold. “It's better now, look at those children, how joyfully they run.”

“Yes, at least we're not starving. There are more things in the shops too, though you still have to queue.” He took a cigarette pack from his pocket, hesitated, then put it back. “I hear wages are going up again next month, for engineers and technicians.”

“Mm-hmm,” she responded. “My son works at that new factory. He says it's very busy, but the pay is decent.”

They fell silent again, only the children's laughter and the distant city bustle flowing in the air. A breeze blew, carrying a hint of early autumn coolness.

“Do you think… if Alexei could see it now, what would he think?” he suddenly asked, his voice much lower.

Her body trembled almost imperceptibly. Her gaze, fixed on the distance, became somewhat misty. “He… he always said, one day it would be better. One day, we could sing freely in the square, without fear of prying ears.” Her eyes welled up, but she fought back the tears. “He waited his whole life…”

He too fell silent. He took out the cigarette pack again, this time lighting one, taking a deep drag. The smoke slowly dissipated in the golden twilight. The children continued to laugh and play, the tram continued to clang, and life seemed to be flowing towards a better direction, with an almost dull resilience.

He looked at this companion beside him, so familiar yet somewhat strange. Decades of hardship had etched similar lines on their faces, and also separated them with too many unspoken stories.

“By the way,” he suddenly spoke, with a hint of bewilderment, “did we… know each other before? Who were you again?”

She turned her head, tears finally sliding silently down her cheeks, yet her face wore a smile of release, a smile that held infinite.

options.name: A name, and us, who lived on.

title: Belarusian Reconstruction Committee Work Directive
desc:
To: Comrade Director, Belarusian Provisional Reconstruction Committee

From: Belov, Section Four, Reconstruction Guidance Office, Central Planning Bureau

Subject: Preliminary Instructions for Initiating the First Phase of Reconstruction Work in the Belarusian Region

Comrade Director,
Preliminary instructions regarding the reconstruction work in the Belarusian region are hereby issued. The Central Committee places great hope in your committee, expecting you to rapidly reverse the difficult situation in the region caused by long-term devastation by fascist bandits and their puppet regimes.

The current top priorities are: One, to comprehensively assess and report on infrastructure damage, especially transportation, energy, and communication networks in key cities like Minsk and Gomel. Two, to inventory and register remaining industrial facilities and agricultural resources, establish a baseline, and provide a basis for subsequent planning. Three, to immediately begin restoring crucial livelihood guarantees, stabilize social order, particularly food supply and basic medical care. Four, in coordination with security departments, to resolutely eliminate remaining hostile elements and sabotage activities.

The Central Committee is well aware of the arduous tasks and limited resources, but the heroic spirit and indomitable perseverance demonstrated by the Belarusian people during the Great Patriotic War are our invaluable assets in overcoming all difficulties. It is imperative to fully mobilize and rely on the masses, using limited resources where they are most needed. Initial aid supplies (including construction materials, seeds, medical supplies) will be allocated progressively starting next month.

Please have your committee promptly submit a detailed status report and a draft work plan for the first phase (the next six months). Subsequent support will be arranged based on specific circumstances and the overall national unified plan. Remember, efficiency and stability are equally important.

title: New Life in the Cowshed
desc:
The morning mist had not yet dissipated when the 'Red Star' collective farm on the outskirts of Brest awoke. Masha, the farm's veterinary assistant, was carefully examining a calf born just a few days ago. This little black-and-white fellow was the twelfth new life welcomed by the farm in recent months, and the fifth Masha had personally delivered.

The cowshed was still the same old cowshed. The Germans had requisitioned it during the occupation, and some faint German graffiti still remained in the corners. The roof leaked, and the hay on the floor wasn't thick enough. But at least, with fewer cows, it felt more spacious. Moreover, in a corner were piled several sacks of feed printed with unfamiliar Cyrillic letters—supposedly “high-protein nutritional supplements” allocated from above. Though the cows were initially reluctant to eat it, their milk yield did increase afterward.

“Look at you, little one, quite sturdy!” Masha gently patted the calf's back, and the calf affectionately nuzzled her hand. “When you grow up, you’ll help us produce more milk and till more land.” Her voice was full of hope, as if she were looking at her own child.

Old Ivan, the farm chairman, limped over, holding a chipped enamel mug. “Comrade Masha, take a break, have some hot tea.” He handed her the mug and looked at the group of calves milling around their mothers, a rare smile on his face. “A good omen, these little ones. It feels like the whole farm has come alive since they arrived.”

“Yes, Comrade Chairman,” Masha took the mug, the warmth dispelling some of the chill. “It's just that the cows' milk is still not quite enough. If only we could get more good feed, or… or introduce a few high-yield breeding cows.”

“We will, Comrade Masha, we will have them all.” Old Ivan gazed eastward, towards the rising sun, and also towards Minsk and Moscow. “Everything is slowly getting better. We lost so much, but as long as these little ones can be born and grow up, there’s hope for these days.”

options.name: Every moo echoes the land's desire.

title: Medals in a Glass Case
desc:
In central Minsk, a renovated building, its facade still bearing some scars of war, once again displayed the sign “Belarusian History Museum.” Irina, a young history graduate now working as a museum guide, was leading a small group of visiting students.

The exhibition hall was spacious and bright, impeccably clean. But the exhibits seemed somewhat… sparse. Many glass cases were empty or contained only photocopies of photos and documents. War and looting had taken too much. Irina focused her explanation on the “Great Patriotic War and the Belarusian People’s Resistance” section. Here, rusty rifles, scorched military uniforms, crude radios used by partisans, and a few Red Star medals that had survived the war were displayed.

“Class, please look,” Irina pointed to a “Partisan of the Great Patriotic War” medal resting on a velvet cushion, her voice clear and tinged with deliberately suppressed emotion. “This medal belonged to a hero named Vasily. During the German occupation, he and his comrades fought under the harshest conditions, disrupting enemy transport lines and protecting our compatriots. Every forest in Belarus was a fortress of their resistance.”

A small boy in the front row raised his hand: “Teacher, why were the Germans so bad?”

Irina paused, choosing her words carefully. “Because… they were blinded by an evil ideology called ‘Fascism.’ They believed they were a superior race and could freely oppress and enslave other nations. But history has proven that justice will eventually triumph over evil. Our great motherland and heroic people ultimately crushed the fascist bandits.”

The narrative was standardized, emphasizing resistance, sacrifice, ultimate victory, and the current rebirth under a unified banner. Cruel details of the war, complex motives of collaborators, and policy vacillations during different periods… these were carefully omitted or simplified. History, like the museum itself, always selectively displayed the parts it wished to be seen.

At the end of the tour, Irina saw an elderly, white-haired man standing alone before Vasily’s medal display case, silent for a long time, his shoulders trembling slightly. She didn’t approach him. Some memories, museum glass cases cannot fully contain.

options.name: History is wiped clean, but still feels rough to the touch.

title: 'Red Star' Breeding Pigs Arrive at the Farm
desc:
The state-run pig farm on the outskirts of Gomel was having a big day. Several new GAZ trucks carefully drove into the farm area, stopping in front of the newly built, whitewashed pigsties. The truck doors opened, and amidst excited chatter and the oinking of pigs, a group of plump, glossy-coated 'Large White pigs' were herded out.

“Comrades, look!” The farm manager, a short, stout but energetic middle-aged man, waved his arms at the workers and technicians. “This is the superior ‘Ukrainian Large White’ breed imported from our Ukrainian brothers! High yield! Disease resistant! Fast growing! With them, our Belarusian pork production will surely skyrocket!”

A technician, holding a notebook, carefully recorded the number and characteristics of each breeding pig, occasionally prodding those that seemed listless with a small stick. “Comrade Manager, long-distance transport has affected them considerably. They need to be quarantined and observed immediately, and their nutrition supplemented.”

“Of course, of course! Comrade, these precious darlings are in your hands!” The manager thumped his chest in assurance. “Feed will be plentiful! Veterinarians on call! We must ensure they adapt to their new home quickly and produce many offspring! We aim for our pork to be on the tables of Minsk and even Moscow by this time next year!”

The workers, with much ado, herded these 'foreign VIPs' into the clean, spacious new pigsties. These sties were built according to the latest 'scientific breeding standards,' a stark contrast to the old, low, damp pigpens nearby. Old Pyotr, a lifelong pig keeper, watched these white, plump, oinking newcomers, shaking his head, then nodding. He had raised local black-haired native pigs all his life; though they grew slowly, they were hardy and ate anything. These delicate 'Large Whites,' well-fed and well-housed, whether they could adapt to Belarusian conditions was truly uncertain.

However, seeing the manager and technician's energetic demeanor, the new pigsties, and the truckloads of feed, a glimmer of hope also arose in Old Pyotr's heart. Perhaps, this time they could really make something of pig farming? At least, more pigs meant more meat, and life should get a little better, shouldn't it?

options.name: New oinks herald a change on the dinner table.

title: The Collective Farm's 'Tractor Symphony'
desc:
The 'Dawn' collective farm in the Vitebsk region was undergoing a transformation. The farm's size had tripled, incorporating several nearby scattered small farms. The endless fields were replanned, divided into neat, large plots of arable land. Most notably, several new, brightly red-painted tractors had replaced most of the old oxen and draft horses, becoming the protagonists in the fields.

Anton, once the owner of one of those small farms, was now the captain of the 'Dawn' farm's first tractor team.
