He sat high in the driver's seat, feeling the powerful vibrations of the diesel engine beneath him, the freshly turned black earth behind him exuding a refreshing aroma. This felt completely different from plowing with his old horse—faster, stronger, more… powerful. According to the plan, his team was responsible for plowing five hundred hectares today, a task unthinkable in the past.

“Captain Anton!” The farm's technician, a young man with glasses, rode up on his bicycle, waving a form. “Maintain depth! The blueprint requires 25 centimeters! And control fuel consumption, don't exceed the quota!”

Anton nodded, slightly adjusting the plow's depth. Centralized management had its pros and cons. The benefit was unified resource allocation, leading to higher efficiency. The drawback was more rules; everything had to follow the forms, lacking the carefree freedom of farming one's own land. On the adjacent plot, another tractor roared deafeningly. Its driver, a greenhorn, operated it somewhat clumsily, his furrows crooked.

In the distance, some old farmers, not yet fully adapted to collective life, led their emaciated old horses, which they were reluctant to hand over, tilling small, leftover patches of land. Their figures, set against the massive tractors, appeared small and lonely. Anton knew what they were thinking; he himself sometimes missed the old days of modest self-sufficiency. But times had changed. Fragmented small-scale farming couldn't feed so many people, nor could it support national reconstruction. Only by centralizing, by achieving scale, could they truly change their fate.

The tractors advanced tirelessly across the vast fields, their monotonous, powerful roar like a crude yet potent symphony of a new era.

options.name: The roar of engines is the prelude to abandoning old ruts.

title: Will Milk Flow Automatically?
desc:
“A miracle! It’s simply a miracle!” Farmwoman Zoya stared wide-eyed as the humming, silver-white machine skillfully attached itself to the cow’s udders, and then streams of white milk began to flow through the transparent pipes. “It… it can really milk itself?”

“Of course, Aunt Zoya,” the white-coated technician beside her explained with a smile. “This is the latest model ‘Dawn’ electric milking machine. Not only is it fast, but it’s also more hygienic than manual milking and can reduce the incidence of mastitis. From now on, you won’t have to get up before dawn to milk each cow by hand. It saves time and effort!”

Zoya still found it hard to believe. She and her sisters, for generations, had milked cows by hand. It was a task requiring skill and patience, a sense of the cow’s mood, and the right amount of pressure. And now, this cold machine, plugged in, could automatically draw out the milk? She leaned closer; the machine pulsed rhythmically, and the cow seemed comfortable, leisurely chewing its cud.

“With this treasure, our farm’s milk production can increase by at least thirty percent!” the farm secretary exclaimed excitedly nearby. “And it can guarantee quality! In the future, our milk might even be rated a ‘premium product’ and earn us extra bonuses!”

Zoya watched the milk flow through the pipes into a huge stainless steel collection tank, her feelings mixed. It was easier, yes, but she felt something was missing. In the past, when she milked, she would talk to the cows, hum songs, feel their warm bodies and trusting eyes. Now, between human and cow, there was a humming machine. Modernization was good, but would those old emotions and connections slowly disappear along with the calluses on her hands?

options.name: Machines bring efficiency, and also new distances.

title: The Khatyn Forest Memorial
desc:
Khatyn Forest, a land that had witnessed too much bloodshed and suffering, now embraced a solemn moment. On the site of the village burned down by German invaders, a new memorial rose. The main sculpture depicted a mother cradling her dead child, and the pedestal was engraved with a concise, heavy line: “In memory of the Belarusian people who perished in the Great Patriotic War.”

Autumn sunlight filtered through sparse leaves, falling on the crowd gathered for the unveiling ceremony. There were white-haired old partisans, their chests adorned with faded medals; children in new school uniforms, wearing red pioneer scarves; peasants from nearby villages, their faces solemn; and government officials and military representatives in crisp uniforms.

An old partisan, his voice trembling but still strong, stepped onto the makeshift podium. “Comrades, friends,” he scanned the crowd, his gaze sweeping over the land, overgrown with grass yet still exuding an aura of death. “We stand here to remember. To remember the innocent victims whose lives were taken by fascist beasts, to remember the martyrs who fought bravely to defend our homeland. The tragedy of Khatyn village is but a microcosm of countless tragedies in our Belarus. A quarter of our population! We lost a quarter of our compatriots!” His voice choked, and suppressed sobs rippled through the audience.

“But,” he raised his voice, his eyes rekindling with fire, “we did not surrender! Our people resisted in the forests, in the swamps, under the enemy’s bayonets! We shed our blood, but we won the final victory! We drove the German aggressors from our land!”

“Today, we stand on this reborn land to pay tribute to the fallen. Their sacrifice was not in vain! Behold, new villages are built, factory chimneys are smoking, children can study in peace again! We are building a strong, unified motherland! This is the best solace for the martyrs!”

The red cloth was slowly unveiled, revealing the mother statue’s sorrowful yet resolute face to the crowd. No one spoke, only the rustling of wind through the trees and the distant roar of tractors, symbolizing new life. This history was too heavy to forget, impossible to forget. But remembrance was for moving forward better.

options.name: The fallen rest; the living march on.

title: The Old Guardian of Belovezha
desc:
On the edge of the Białowieża Primeval Forest, autumn was in full swing. Forester Yuri Karpovich, a swarthy, taciturn old man, rode his equally aged horse along a barely visible path known only to him. He had worked here for nearly forty years, familiar with every tree, every ravine in the forest. He had seen Tsarist hunting parties, the fires of two world wars, Germans establishing a restricted zone here, and post-war partisans and mopping-up troops chasing each other through this wilderness.

Now, the war was over, and the forest had returned to its ancient tranquility, broken only by the occasional sound of an axe and the distant hubbub of tourists. This vast forest had been declared a 'National Nature Reserve,' and Karpovich's duties had expanded from preventing poaching and fires to guiding tourists and stopping them from littering.

This morning, deep in the forest, he found a string of huge footprints and fresh droppings—European bison! These kings of the forest, nearly hunted to extinction during the war, were now slowly recovering in numbers. Karpovich carefully recorded the location and count, a sense of satisfaction welling up inside him. This forest was his lifelong charge; seeing it revitalized pleased him more than anything.

However, troubles came with it. Yesterday, he caught two 'tourists' from Minsk who actually wanted to hunt wild boar in the forest with shotguns! It took Karpovich a great deal of effort to drag them to the management office. And those city folk who littered bottles and cans, they simply didn't understand the forest's fragility.

“Protect nature… sounds nice,” Karpovich muttered to his old horse, which flicked its tail in agreement. “But if people’s hearts are rotten, even the best reserve is useless.” He sighed and continued his patrol. The forest was vast, quiet; it had witnessed too much human folly and greed, and also tenacious vitality. Perhaps, protecting this forest was also about guarding something more important.

options.name: The forest is silent; it has seen too many rise and fall.

title: The 'Salt' Underground
desc:
The landscape of the Soligorsk mining area was strikingly different from the pastoral scenes elsewhere in Belarus. Massive headframes towered into the sky, conveyor belts snaked like steel pythons, continuously transporting dark brown ore to the processing plant. A faint salty and chemical smell permeated the air. This was a potash mine, one of Belarus's 'underground treasures.'

Vadim, a young miner, had just finished his morning shift. He took off his dust-caked work clothes and washed the grime from his face, revealing a tired but still youthful countenance. In the shower room, he joked with his workmates, complaining about the stifling heat and noise underground, while also dreaming of going to the newly opened cinema in town after payday.

“Heard the news? Production quotas are going up again next month!” a colleague said while toweling off. “They say Moscow is building new fertilizer plants and urgently needs our potash!”

“Let them raise it,” another said nonchalantly. “More work, more pay, it’s better than when the Germans were here. Back then, no matter how much you worked, you were only half-full.”

Vadim said nothing. He remembered when his father worked in this mine as a child. Conditions were worse then, and safety accidents were frequent. His father always said they were exchanging their lives for the country's needs. Now, conditions had indeed improved considerably, with new ventilation equipment and stricter safety regulations. New workers' dormitories and a club had also been built in the mining area. But Vadim always felt that they were still exchanging their sweat, even their health, for the needs of those distant places.

Walking out of the mine gate, the sunlight was somewhat dazzling. He saw several trains, laden with potash fertilizer, slowly departing for unknown destinations. This 'salt,' dug from deep beneath Belarusian soil, would nourish Russia's vast fields, turning into bread, into potatoes, into the cornerstone supporting the entire nation's reconstruction. Perhaps this was the meaning of his work? Vadim揉了揉 his aching shoulders and headed towards town. Tonight, he wanted to see that reportedly spectacular new movie.

options.name: Underground treasures nourish hopes above ground.

title: Gazing at the Other Shore
desc:
Private Timofey Ivanov, a farm boy from Penza Oblast, stood on the newly built border watchtower, the cold wind piercing his ill-fitting, thick greatcoat. This was his third month in Belarus, and his first time being assigned to this outpost, right next to 'the other side.' Barbed wire snaked below, new and glaring, and further out were minefields and freshly dug anti-tank ditches.

Night had fallen. On his side of the land, there were only scattered lights from military barracks and the dim glow of distant villages. But looking west, across the silent river, he could see a continuous stretch of lights, and even faintly hear the roar of truck engines—that was German-controlled territory, once also part of their motherland.

“See anything, kid?” asked old soldier Vasily from below the tower, as he rolled a cigarette. He had been here longer than Timofey had been a soldier and was said to have experienced the most brutal retreats.

“Nothing, Uncle Vasily, just… the lights on the other side are quite bright,” Timofey answered, somewhat nervously.

“Bright? Humph, German lightbulbs might be better, but their lives aren't necessarily comfortable.” Vasily exhaled a thick cloud of smoke. “Don’t be fooled by the lights, kid. The people over there are just like us, also hoping for dawn.” He paused, his voice dropping slightly. “We guard here to ensure that one day, our lights can also illuminate that side, instead of their darkness engulfing us.”

Timofey gripped his rifle tighter; the cold steel gave him a sense of security. He no longer looked at the lights on the other bank but carefully observed the land before him—their land, slowly awakening. The wind seemed to carry the faint sound of tractors tilling at night from a distance, a sound that belonged to them.

options.name: The border river is silent, flowing with waiting and vigilance.

title: Craters in the Birch Forest
desc:
The breath of spring finally descended upon the Belarusian fields; melting snow formed meandering streams across the meadows. Sunlight, filtered through the newly emerged leaves of birch trees, cast dappled shadows. Alyona, a young woman working at a collective farm on the outskirts of Minsk, carried a basket, foraging for the first tender wild mushrooms at the edge of the woods. The air was filled with the fragrance of earth and grass.

This birch forest was as beautiful as a poem, tranquil and full of life. Alyona had played here since childhood, familiar with every tree, every berry bush. Yet she also knew how much pain lay buried beneath this tranquility. Not far away, a huge, moss-covered shell crater, like an ugly scar, marred the harmony of the landscape. During the war, fierce battles had taken place here; German tanks and Soviet artillery had repeatedly ravaged this woodland.

She bent down, carefully parting the fallen leaves, revealing several round, white mushrooms. Just then, she heard a low rumble in the distance—not thunder, but… the sound of machines. Several military trucks, painted green and hauling heavy machinery, slowly drove past the edge of the woods along a newly built dirt road, leaving two deep ruts behind.

Alyona stood up, watching the trucks disappear at the other end of the forest. She knew those machines were bound for the western border, to build new defensive fortifications. To prevent the iron hooves of war from trampling this beautiful land again, people were erecting new barriers of steel and concrete. This made her feel secure, yet also carried a hint of inexplicable loss. This beautiful birch forest, it held so much—nature's gifts, the scars of war, and now, the imprint of preparations for conflict.

options.name: Verdant green, yet unable to conceal the land's memories.

title: Concrete and Makhorka
desc:
“Hey! Andrei! Stop fucking spacing out, hand me that bag of cement! Yes, the one under your arse!”

Foreman Slava’s roar was still clearly audible above the deafening noise of the concrete mixer. Andrei, a young man fresh out of Ryazan technical school, scrambled to lift the heavy bag of cement and stumbled over to the workers pouring the bunker roof. Sweat soaked his shirt, concrete powder clung to his face, making him look like a ghost just emerged from a flour sack.

This was a top-secret national defense construction site somewhere on the western border of Belarus. As far as the eye could see, rolling hills and massive, newly excavated earthworks dominated the landscape. Hundreds upon hundreds of workers, soldiers, and engineers bustled about like ants, pouring concrete, tying rebar, laying cables. According to the huge blueprint posted on the wall, a vast underground fortress complex would be built here, equipped with the latest artillery, missile silos, and command centers, purported to withstand “any scale of ground attack.”

During the lunch break, Andrei sat with a few fellow workers on a newly poured concrete bunker, sharing black bread and dried salted fish. “Fucking exhausting,” complained a muscular man with a tank tattooed on his arm. “Can’t even see a woman in this damn place. At night, it’s either drinking or playing cards.”

“Quit whining, Misha,” another, slightly older worker said, rolling a makhorka cigarette. “We’re lucky to be working here. Heard this is the country’s most important project, directly related to whether we can stop the Germans. We sweat a bit more now, so we bleed less later.”

Andrei ate his bread in silence. He had studied bridge engineering, expecting to repair bridges over the Dnieper after graduation, but instead, he was assigned to this godforsaken place to dig holes. Every day, he faced cold concrete, deafening noise, and Foreman Slava’s incessant shouting. But he also knew in his heart that the old worker was right. He had seen the ruins left by the war with his own eyes, heard elders recount the humiliation and fear of occupation. If this concrete could really prevent all that from happening again, then no matter how hard or tiring, it was worth it.

He looked up and saw on the distant horizon the silhouette of a new missile silo slowly taking shape against the setting sun, like a silent, resolute finger pointing west.

options.name: A spade of earth, a single brick; building a wall, and also resolve.

title: Pravda: The Alarm Bell Tolls Loudly
desc:
Headline: With Steel Will, Forge the Nation's Barrier—Commemorating the Painful Lessons of the Great Patriotic War



Last night's west wind, sweeping through the streets and alleys of Minsk, brought not biting cold, but the warmth of rebuilding homes. Factory chimneys stand tall again, tractors sing in the fields, classrooms echo with children's reading. The banner of victory flies high above the republic, the dawn of peace seemingly illuminates this land ravaged by suffering.

However, comrades, friends! We must not indulge in the current tranquility and forget the unforgettable pain! We must not forget how, in the not-too-distant past, the iron heel of fascism trampled our homeland, how barbaric flames engulfed our cities and villages! We must not forget what a terrible price Belarus, this heroic land, paid—a quarter of the population sacrificed! Every inch of land is soaked with the blood of martyrs and the tears of the innocent!

Forty years of tyranny, forty years of humiliation! The lessons of history are like an alarm bell that must toll loudly in each of our hearts! “Past experience, if not forgotten, is a guide for the future.” We paid a bloody price for lack of preparation; our families were shattered because of the enemy's brutality. Such tragedies must never be allowed to happen again!

Yes, we achieved a great victory, driving the invaders from our borders. But the threat from the West has not been eliminated; the ambition of imperialism still exists. They may be dormant for now, but their wolfish ambition to covet our land and attempt to subvert our cause has never changed!

Therefore, we must, with hundredfold vigilance and thousandfold effort, turn our western frontier, turn our heroic Belarus, into an indestructible steel barrier! We must arm our army with the most advanced weapons, defend our borders with the strongest fortifications! We must make every soldier a vigilant sentry, make every inch of land an insurmountable grave for invaders!

“Never again shall we be invaded!” This is not just a slogan; it is our solemn promise to the fallen martyrs, our historical responsibility to future generations, an iron oath forged with blood and life! Let the alarm bell toll loudly, let our will be like steel! For the eternal consolidation of the motherland, for the lasting peace, for our free and happy life, be always prepared!

options.name: Belarus stands at the forefront, never retreating.

title: The Last Potatoes
desc:
Lyuba looked at the lonely plate of boiled potatoes on the dinner table, then at the three children sitting around it—their little faces full of longing as they stared at the meager amount of food. Her husband Alexei, the tractor driver who used to be as strong as a bear, was now thinner too, silently smoking a cigarette.

This winter was particularly harsh. Last year's harvest was decent, but most of the grain was requisitioned under the pretext of 'supporting frontline construction.' The town's factories were the same; workshops that originally produced farm tools and daily necessities were now converted to making military parts. Machines roared day and night, but the workers' rations grew smaller and smaller.

“Mama, I want a little more…” her youngest son Sasha whispered.

Lyuba stroked his head tenderly, picking the largest potato from the plate and putting it in his bowl. “Eat, Sasha, eat more and grow tall.” She herself had no appetite.

The neighbor's son, only seventeen, was drafted last month and sent to the western border. The boy's mother cried for days. Everyone knew the country was preparing for a possible war; the 'military-first policy' was mentioned daily in the newspapers. Sacrifices were necessary for the country's security, to avoid being bullied by the Germans again. She understood the rationale, but seeing her children's sallow faces, seeing her husband's increasingly gaunt shoulders, her heart ached as if gripped by something painful.

After dinner, Alexei silently took out his tools and began repairing the old tractor that had accompanied him for years. “Heard they’re organizing ‘voluntary labor’ in the spring to help the army build fortifications,” he said in a low voice. “At home… I’m relying on you.”

Lyuba nodded without speaking. She walked to the window, gazing at the silent, moonlit village outside. Faint bugle calls seemed to drift from the direction of the military camp. Security was important, but what about life? Must they live like this for the sake of supposed security? She didn't know the answer, only that tomorrow's potatoes might be even fewer.

options.name: To make the shield strong enough, we tightened our belts.

title: Bunkers and Lullabies
desc:
On the western outskirts of Minsk, near the new defense line, the nights were exceptionally quiet, but also exceptionally… oppressive. Irina gently rocked the baby in her arms, humming an old Belarusian lullaby. Her husband Peter, an engineer, worked in the huge underground command center nearby, codenamed 'Bear's Den,' and hadn't been home for almost a month.

Outside the window, faint concrete outlines could be seen under camouflage netting on the distant hills, and searchlight beams occasionally swept across the night sky. During the day, the roar of construction machinery and the commands of drilling soldiers often filled the air. They said this place was the nation's strongest shield, built to protect ordinary people like her and her child.

Irina knew Peter's work was important and arduous. But every time he returned, he seemed more silent and tired, a kind of anxiety she couldn't understand in his eyes. He said it was heavily guarded inside, isolated from the world, like living in a giant steel can. He said it was safe there, indestructible.

But Irina didn't feel very safe. Living on the edge of this giant 'fortress,' she always felt surrounded, not by enemies, but by the cold walls they had built themselves and the ubiquitous watchful eyes. Neighbors spoke in lower voices, and children were told not to go near the military restricted zones. An invisible tension seemed to permeate the air, making even the lullaby's melody feel heavy.

The baby in her arms finally fell asleep, breathing evenly and peacefully. Irina carefully placed him in the cradle. She went to the window, gazing at the massive fortifications looming faintly in the darkness. Could they really bring safety? Or did they merely weld the fear and shadow of war deeper into their lives?

options.name: Within high walls, is it peace, or a cage?

title: The Veteran's Rifle
desc:
Dust swirled on the training ground as a group of fresh-faced recruits in brand-new uniforms practiced shooting. Gunshots echoed, but stray bullets clearly outnumbered hits. Old instructor Dmitri Pavlovich, a veteran who had lost an arm at Stalingrad, paced back and forth behind the line, leaning on his cane, his brow furrowed.

“Worthless! A bunch of worthless maggots!” he finally roared, his voice hoarse yet powerful. “Is that how you shoot? Are you trying to tickle the enemy? Are your eyes on your arse?!” The recruits flinched, ceasing fire.

“Listen up, lads!” Pavlovich strode to the firing line, snatching a rifle from a recruit. His movements were somewhat clumsy, but his eyes were sharp as a hawk’s. “Do you think war is a game? Think the enemy will stand still for you to aim?” He took a deep breath, seemingly recalling something. “Let me tell you, back then, in the summer of ’41, when the Germans fired the first shot, many of us hadn’t even held a rifle! Many didn’t even know which way to run!”

His voice dropped, filled with visceral pain. “My company, one hundred and twenty good lads, half were gone the first day! They didn’t even see what the enemy looked like! Planes swarmed like locusts, tanks rolled over us like monsters! We weren’t prepared, we were caught completely off guard! Rivers of blood, lads! Do you know what that feels like?”

Dead silence fell over the training ground, only the wind whistling across the empty field. The recruits looked at the tears and fire flickering in the one-armed veteran’s eyes, seemingly feeling the suffocating weight of that disaster.

“Now,” Pavlovich raised the rifle again, steady as a rock despite having only one arm, “we have time to prepare, we have enough weapons, we have strong fortifications! We’ve learned our lesson! We must not be like headless flies again when the first shot is fired! Every bullet in your hands could decide a comrade’s life, decide whether we can defend the homeland behind us! Did you all hear me clearly?!”

“Yes, Instructor!” The recruits’ answer was uniform and loud, filled with unprecedented determination. Pavlovich nodded, handed the rifle back to the recruit. “Now, reload! Aim properly! Remember, we are no longer the unprepared army of the past!”

title: The Air Raid Drill
desc:
At precisely three o'clock in the afternoon, the shrill, piercing sound of air raid sirens abruptly filled the skies over Gomel. People on the streets paused for a moment, then began moving methodically towards the nearest underground shelters. It wasn't a real air raid, just a routine weekly drill. But even knowing it was a drill, the familiar, heart-stopping sound still made many hearts skip a beat.

Mikhail, a shop assistant at a state-run store, expertly locked the shop door, grabbed the first-aid kit hanging on the wall, and hurried towards the corner subway station entrance—which also served as the designated public shelter. He saw his neighbor, old Anton, supporting his frail wife with difficulty as they slowly descended the stairs. A group of Young Pioneers in red scarves, led by their teacher, walked in neat lines, their small faces showing some nervousness but no panic.

The subway platform had been temporarily converted into a shelter. The lighting was dim, the air somewhat stuffy. People leaned against each other, sitting or standing, talking in low voices. A few soldiers maintained order, their expressions serious but not hostile. Propaganda posters adorned the walls, illustrating how to identify different types of bombs and how to perform self-rescue during an air raid.

“Another drill,” Mikhail heard someone nearby complain softly. “It’s been peaceful for so many years, why still do this? Could the Germans really attack again?”

“Shh! Be careful!” another person immediately hushed him. “The newspaper says imperialism’s ambition to destroy us has not died! We must always remain vigilant! Have you forgotten the lesson of Khatyn?”

Mikhail didn’t join their discussion. He just leaned against the cold wall, silently observing it all. This state of “always being prepared” had become a part of their lives. It was reflected in the weekly siren drills, in the content about patriotism and national defense in children’s textbooks, in the increasing number of military recruitment posters on the streets, and in the subconsciously lowered voices and solemn expressions when people talked about the “western border.”

Peace was real; factories were producing, shops were open, people were falling in love, marrying, having children. But the shadow of war had never truly dissipated; it lingered like a lurking ghost, constantly hanging over this land that had just risen from the ruins. Half an hour later, the short whistle signaling the all-clear sounded. People breathed a sigh of relief, gradually emerging from the subway station back into the sunlight, continuing their unfinished work and lives. As if nothing had happened, yet as if something had quietly been etched into everyone’s bones.

options.name: The string remains taut, waiting for the moment.

title: Song Beneath the Cranes
desc:
In the center of Minsk, former ruins were being replaced by a forest of giant cranes and scaffolding. Vadim, a young construction worker, stood with his colleagues high on the scaffolding, securing prefabricated concrete panels. The sun was dazzling; the air filled with the smell of new cement, welding sparks, and workers' sweat. Below, the streets bustled with traffic, newly paved asphalt roads glistened darkly, and brand-new trolleybuses glided silently past, their windows reflecting the rising Soviet-style apartment buildings and glass-fronted public buildings on either side.
“Hey, Vadim! What are you daydreaming about? Pass that rebar over here!” the foreman shouted.

Vadim snapped back to reality, handing over a heavy bundle of rebar. “Foreman, do you think… when this building is finished, we’ll really get to live in new apartments?” he asked, wiping sweat from his brow, a little uncertainly. He still lived with his parents and sister in an old, repeatedly repaired building on the outskirts.
“Nonsense! It was in the newspaper! Priority allocation for us builders!” The foreman grinned, showing white teeth. “When this ‘Victory’ Avenue is finished, my old woman will be able to plant flowers on the balcony! I’ll invite you over for a housewarming drink then!”

The workers burst into good-natured laughter. In the distance, singing drifted over—a group of children in red scarves, led by their teacher, were visiting the construction site. They sang songs about construction, about the future, their clear, bright voices cutting through the site's noise. Vadim paused his work, listening for a moment. He imagined the future; perhaps in this very building he was helping to construct, his own children could sing so carefree.

The crane’s boom slowly rose, lifting a huge wall panel high into the air, as if stitching the final wound of this city reborn from fire, and also outlining the shape of the future.

options.name: Brick by brick, laying the foundation for tomorrow.

title: Concerto of Field and Chimney
desc:
In Brest Oblast, Andrei Petrovich, chairman of the 'October Harvest' collective farm, was arguing loudly into the phone, his face flushed red: “What? Half the tractors are being transferred again? To support the expansion of some… ‘Second Chemical Plant’? Can you eat chemical plants? Spring plowing is about to start! We were counting on them to plant more grain!”

A bored bureaucratic voice came from the other end: “Comrade Andrei, these are orders from the Central Committee! Industrialization is the priority task! Chemical plants produce fertilizer, which ultimately increases grain yields! You need to see the bigger picture!”

Andrei almost slammed the phone down in anger. The bigger picture? His bigger picture was the hundreds of hungry mouths on the farm and the meager grain reserves left in the warehouse after handing over most of last year's harvest! City factories were important, sure, but if crops couldn’t grow in the fields, what use was more fertilizer?

After hanging up, he paced irritably in his office. Outside the window lay the freshly plowed black earth, exuding a moist aroma; the few remaining tractors moved slowly. Further in the distance, several towering chimneys pierced the horizon—the sign of the newly built 'Second Chemical Plant,' relentlessly spewing greyish-white smoke into the sky day and night.

Just then, the farm’s technician, a young graduate from the agricultural college, rushed in excitedly. “Comrade Chairman! Good news! The higher-ups have approved our trial of ‘straw return’ and ‘scientific crop rotation’ technologies! They say it can improve soil fertility without needing much fertilizer!”

Andrei was愣住 for a moment. He looked at the light shining in the young man's eyes, then at the vast fields and distant chimneys outside the window. Maybe… maybe there really was a way for the fields and chimneys to stop competing for resources, and instead, jointly play a concerto of development? His tightly knitted brow finally relaxed slightly.

options.name: Between the furrow and the assembly line, searching for that delicate balance.

title: Not Just Potato Peels Anymore
desc:
Nadezhda carefully added a small spoonful of white sugar to her daughter Katya’s teacup, watching the crystalline granules slowly dissolve. Katya’s eyes widened in surprise as she looked at her mother: “Mama, today… can we use sugar?”

“Of course, my little beet,” Nadezhda smiled, stroking her daughter’s hair. “Today is Papa’s payday, and he brought this back too!” She took a tin box decorated with colorful candy wrappers from the cupboard—it contained fruit candies newly produced by the Gomel Candy Factory, something seen only during New Year or when hosting important guests in the past.

Her husband Mikhail, the old lathe operator who had diligently worked at the bearing factory for twenty years, sat at the table watching his wife and daughter, a contented smile on his face. He remembered the hard times: war, famine, rationing, never knowing where the next meal would come from. In the most difficult times, they even had to boil potato peels to stave off hunger. His daughter Katya had barely tasted sweetness growing up.

But now, things were truly different. Though far from wealthy, at least they no longer worried about starving. The shop shelves slowly held more items: fabric, soap, even occasionally a bit of sausage. Last year, they moved into a new apartment allocated by the factory; it was small, but had a separate kitchen and bathroom, and heating in winter. Mikhail’s wages had also increased twice; though not much, it was enough for Nadezhda to occasionally buy Katya a piece of fruit candy.

“Papa,” Katya unwrapped a candy wrapper, popped the shiny sweet into her mouth, and closed her eyes happily, “this is really sweet!”

Mikhail watched his daughter’s contented face, his heart filled with warmth. The shadow of poverty had not completely disappeared, and the burdens of life remained heavy. But at least, they could now taste a little sweetness. For this small sweetness, for the hope that his daughter could eat candy every day in the future, he felt all the hardship was worthwhile.

options.name: The taste of life is quietly sweetening.

title: Flags on Victory Square
desc:
Minsk, Victory Square. Bright sunshine, colorful flags fluttering. Tens of thousands gathered here for the grand rally celebrating the 'Exhibition of Belarusian Liberation and Reconstruction Achievements.' Majestic marches blared from loudspeakers, and honor guards in brand-new uniforms marched past with crisp, powerful steps. On the viewing stands sat government officials, military generals, labor models, and representatives from 'fraternal republics.'

In the center of the square, on a temporary platform, Belarus's 'glorious achievements' in reconstruction were displayed: models of new tractors produced by the Minsk Tractor Works, photos of BelAZ heavy trucks, ore samples from the Soligorsk Potash Plant, and beautiful linen cloth with national patterns woven by female textile workers. Detailed descriptions accompanied each exhibit, emphasizing how, under the Party's leadership, the Belarusian people overcame difficulties, relied on their own efforts, and achieved world-renowned successes.

Sixteen-year-old Viktor and his classmates were also squeezed into the crowd, excitedly waving small flags. Their teacher told them to be proud of being part of the 'great Belarus.' Watching the imposing soldiers, the gleaming machine models, and listening to the impassioned speeches from the loudspeakers, Viktor indeed felt a surge of hot blood. He was proud of the rebirth of the land beneath his feet, moved by the toil of the builders.

However, an elderly woman with white hair standing beside him just watched quietly, her eyes showing no excitement, only a complex and profound emotion. Viktor noticed a strip of black mourning cloth peeking from her sleeve. Perhaps, for her, the square's hustle and bustle and colorful flags could not completely cover the recent wounds and losses.

The climax of the rally arrived. A huge red flag slowly rose above the square, and the crowd erupted in thunderous applause and cheers. Shouts of “Hurrah! Hurrah!” echoed through the sky. Viktor shouted along, believing the future must be bright, great. Yet, within that greatness, there seemed to be some subtle, heavy echoes belonging to the past.

options.name: Beneath the banner, lies glory, and also undried tears.

title: Whispers in the Library
desc:
The newly built National Library of Belarus, spacious and bright, filled with the scent of books. Huge glass windows let the afternoon sun into the reading room, illuminating the young students hunched over their desks. Only the rustling of turning pages and the occasional deliberately suppressed cough broke the silence.

Svetlana, a university student studying linguistics, was immersed in a newly published anthology of modern Belarusian poetry. This was unthinkable just a few years ago. Back then, many native writers' names were taboo, and bookstores were filled with monotonous propaganda pamphlets and leader's quotations. Now, although censorship still existed, at least some of their own voices were beginning to be allowed expression again.

She read a poem describing the morning in her hometown, the language simple yet beautiful, evoking childhood memories. She looked up and saw the reading room filled with faces as young as hers, engrossed in thick scientific works or quietly discussing literature, their eyes shining with the light of knowledge and aspiration for the future. Yes, a new era was dawning, full of opportunities and possibilities, as if after all the dust had settled, the sun had finally broken through the haze.

“Hello, may I sit here?” a soft voice interrupted her thoughts. It was a boy about her age, clutching several thick philosophy books.

“Of course,” Svetlana smiled, moving her books aside.

After sitting down, the boy hesitated, then asked in a low voice, “Are you reading Kupala?”

Svetlana looked up in surprise. “You know him too?”

The boy smiled, a sly glint in his eyes. “Of course, though many of his works still can’t be found in the library.” He leaned closer, his voice even lower. “But, I have some friends… we privately exchange some ‘interesting’ things. Would you like to join?”

Svetlana’s heart beat a little faster. She knew what this ‘private exchange’ meant, and the risks involved. But looking at the mixture of passion, rebellion, and idealism shining in the boy's eyes, she felt an inexplicable attraction. Perhaps, the real ‘brilliance’ came not only from the officially sanctioned light, but also from those sparks of warmth and thought quietly passed around in corners?

options.name: As pages turn, ideas begin to flow silently.

title: Returning Footsteps
desc:
At the end of the dusty road lay the village on the outskirts of Vitebsk he had left decades ago. Alexei Petrovich, a limping veteran with frost-tipped hair, finally stood under the old, crooked willow tree at the village entrance—exactly as he remembered it, only the trunk was thicker, the branches more lush. The war, and the long, distant 'service' after the war, had consumed almost his entire life. Now, he was back, wearing a faded old uniform and carrying a heart both weary and filled with trepidation.

The village had changed. Many low adobe houses were gone, replaced by rows of whitewashed new brick houses with brand-new television antennas on their roofs. Children in clean clothes chased a leather ball in the mud, their laughter crisp and loud, seemingly memory-less of war and hunger. The rhythmic chugging of a tractor drifted from the distance—the direction of the collective farm where he had toiled in his youth. The air carried the mixed scent of freshly baked bread and hay, the smell of peacetime.

He walked slowly down the village's only main road, his steps somewhat unsteady. Passing the once-familiar neighbors' houses, now occupied by faces he didn't recognize, they cast curious and friendly glances his way, but no one recognized him as the young lad who had left from here. He couldn't even find his old family home; a brand-new village club stood in its place, movie posters and agricultural technology promotion flyers pasted on its door.

Everything was so unfamiliar, yet faintly shadowed with familiarity. Like himself—the blood of this land still flowed in his veins, but his soul was long etched with indelible grooves of time and experience, somewhat out of step with the thriving scene before him. He felt like a ghost, hovering between past and present.

He found a stone on the riverbank near the village and sat down, watching the setting sun paint the clouds crimson, also dyeing the quietly flowing river red. Several young people, carrying farm tools, walked past him laughing and talking, heading towards the village. One of them saw him, hesitated, then stopped and asked in a local Russian accent, “Uncle, are you… visiting relatives? It's getting dark, would you like to come to my place for some hot tea?”

Alexei looked up, seeing the young, simple, vibrant face contrasting sharply with his own clouded, weary eyes. He opened his mouth to say something, but found his throat choked. Home… he was finally home. But was this still his home? Could he still integrate into this land that was striving forward, seemingly having forgotten him?

He took a deep breath of the air, filled with the smell of earth and cooking smoke, and slowly nodded. Perhaps this was the so-called 'leap of faith'—believing that this land could accept not only scars but also returning, faltering souls.

options.name: The land beneath his feet, both destination and starting point.

title: Guiding Opinions on Carrying Out Reconstruction Work in Ukrainian Territory
desc:
To: Responsible Comrades at all levels of the Ukrainian Reconstruction Committee
From: Radchenko, Ukrainian Affairs Office, Central Restoration and Development Committee
Subject: Directives and Principles for Initiating the First Phase of Reconstruction Work in the Ukrainian Region
Comrades,
Following the latest directives from the Central Committee, the following guiding opinions on reconstruction work in the Ukrainian region are hereby issued: Ukraine, our former 'breadbasket,' fraternal land, having suffered long and brutal rule and destruction by fascist bandits and their running dogs, is in dire need of reconstruction, with widespread devastation and destitution. The complexity, arduousness, and importance of its reconstruction work cannot be overemphasized. Primary tasks: One, swiftly restore key infrastructure in central cities like Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Dnipropetrovsk, especially transportation, power supply, and communication systems, ensuring economic arteries are unblocked in the shortest possible time. Two, comprehensively inventory agricultural resources, register land, tally farm tools and livestock, and formulate detailed recovery plans for spring planting and autumn harvest; the grain issue is of paramount importance. Three, consolidate remaining industry, particularly coal mines and metallurgical enterprises in the Donbas region, prioritizing the production of materials needed for repairs. Four, stabilize social order, soothe public sentiment, and severely crack down on all hostile activities that disrupt reconstruction and create division. Five, pay special attention to identifying and eliminating the residual toxins of the German occupation colonial rule period, rebuilding a healthy social atmosphere and national identity. The Central Committee fully understands the difficulties you face but firmly believes that the heroic Ukrainian people possess boundless strength. Initial supplies of seeds, fertilizer, medical materials, and basic construction materials will be gradually dispatched following this directive. Your committee is requested to immediately organize forces, conduct in-depth research based on the principle of seeking truth from facts, and promptly submit more detailed status reports and specific work plans. Remember, speed is important, but quality is paramount; rebuild homes, but more importantly, unite hearts.

options.name: Let the Dnieper once again surge with the waves of construction.

title: German Lesson Beneath the Street Sign
desc:
On the cobblestone streets of Lviv's Old Town, several adolescents gathered around a newly installed bilingual street sign, pointing and chattering curiously. Above was the Ukrainian “Rynok Square,” below it a smaller line in Russian, and even further down, faint Gothic German letters, “Marktplatz,” could be discerned beneath a layer of scraped-off paint. Sunlight bathed the ancient stone buildings, structures that had witnessed the changing of too many flags.
Suddenly, a young man wearing a red armband, a member of the “Team for Eliminating Fascist Remnants,” approached. “Little comrades, what are you looking at?” he asked with a smile.
“Uncle, what does the German writing underneath mean?” a bold child asked, pointing at the blurry imprint.
The young man’s smile froze for a second, then his expression turned serious. “That’s the language of the invaders, the filthy mark left by the fascist bandits who oppressed our Ukrainian people! We scraped it off, just like we drove them away! Now, only the languages of our fraternal nations are here!”
The children nodded, seemingly understanding, yet not quite. Just then, an old cobbler sitting nearby looked up and muttered in heavily accented Ukrainian, “Scraped off the letters, can’t scrape off the days…” His voice was low, but loud enough for the young man to hear.
The young man’s face flushed red. He wanted to retort, but looking at the old man’s weathered face, he eventually just snorted and turned to inspect the next street sign. The children scattered too, resuming their game of chasing pigeons. Only the new street sign, and the historical traces beneath it that couldn't be completely erased, stood silently at the street corner, bathed in sunlight and the gazes of passersby.

options.name: New paint can cover old marks, but memories seep through the cracks.

title: The First Furrow
desc:
The vast black earth of Poltava finally welcomed its tractor. Oksana, a swarthy peasant woman with strong arms, was awkwardly but excitedly driving a 'Belarus' brand tractor, newly assigned to the village. It was her first time operating this iron beast that belched black smoke and roared loudly. Behind her, the plow turned over the dark, glistening soil, releasing a refreshing fragrance, as if a giant who had slept too long was finally stretching.
Her husband Petro, leading several young men, followed behind, scattering high-yield wheat seeds supposedly transported from the 'Center.' During the war, this fertile land was either forced to grow industrial raw materials needed by the Germans or simply lay fallow. Petro himself had been captured and forced to build fortifications for the Germans, escaping death by a hair's breadth. Now, being able to sow wheat again on his own (though now called collective farm) land felt like a dream.
“Oksana! Slow down! Don’t bury the seeds too deep!” Petro shouted towards the tractor, a smile on his face. Oksana waved back at him, the tractor's roar drowning out her reply.
In the distance, village elders and children stood on the field ridges, watching the scene. A white-haired old woman made the sign of the cross, muttering words, seemingly praying for this year's harvest. Several children chased the dust kicked up by the tractor, playing joyfully. The sun was warm, the sky blue; the traumatized land was reawakening with life. Though tools were scarce, seeds not quite plentiful, and tractor drivers needed training, the first furrow had been plowed, the seeds of hope had been sown.

options.name: The black earth is silent, awaiting the echo of harvest.

title: New Look for the 'Liberator' Monument
desc:
In the center of Kyiv, the massive granite obelisk erected by the Germans to commemorate their 'liberation of Ukraine from the Bolsheviks' was now shrouded in scaffolding and canvas. Workers were busy hammering and chiseling on it, occasionally sending down fragments of stone. A crowd of onlookers had gathered, pointing and discussing the spectacle.
“Finally, they’re tearing it down!” exclaimed an old man with white hair, leaning on his cane excitedly. “Having this thing standing here is just bad luck! A damn monument left by the German devils!”
“I heard they’re modifying it, not tearing it down,” corrected a man nearby who looked like an intellectual, speaking in a low voice. “The authorities plan to convert it into the ‘Monument to Victory in the Anti-Fascist War,’ keeping the main structure, knocking off the Nazi symbols, and replacing them with statues of our heroes.”
“Modify? Humph, same soup, different bowl!” The old man was clearly unconvinced. “If you ask me, they should blow it up! Into pieces! Let those fascists see who the real masters are!”
“Old man, you can’t say that,” the intellectual pushed up his glasses. “This is also part of history. Keeping it as a negative example, to remind future generations not to forget past suffering, isn’t that better?”
A low murmur of discussion arose from the crowd; clearly, both views had supporters. Some felt complete destruction was necessary for catharsis, while others believed modification and repurposing held more meaning. But regardless, the monument symbolizing humiliation and oppression was about to change its appearance, which in itself was a gesture of victory. Under the setting sun, the silhouettes of workers moved across the massive monument, the sound of hammering like a belated, jarring yet powerful funeral march for the dark era gone by.

options.name: Chisel off the eagle, carve the five-pointed star.

title: Cranes on Khreshchatyk Street
desc:
Kyiv's Khreshchatyk Street, once hailed as the 'most beautiful street in the Soviet Union,' was almost leveled during the war. Now, it had transformed into a gigantic construction site. Crane arms swung through the air, trucks laden with bricks and cement shuttled back and forth, welding sparks flew, and the sounds of hammering, chanting, and roaring machinery blended into a noisy yet vibrant symphony of reconstruction.
Svetlana, a young female engineer wearing a hard hat and holding blueprints, stood before the frame of a newly erected building, gesturing to several dust-covered construction workers. “The reinforcing steel specifications for this load-bearing wall must be correct! And those prefabricated panels over there, the joints must align perfectly! Safety first, but quality must also be guaranteed!” Her voice was clear and firm, standing out remarkably on a predominantly male construction site.
She came from Kharkiv, one of the first technical personnel to respond to the national call and participate in Kyiv's reconstruction. The scene before her both excited her and filled her with immense pressure. The Kyiv on the blueprints was magnificent, imbued with neoclassical grandeur and aspirations for the future. But the reality was widespread devastation, material shortages, a lack of skilled workers, and sometimes frustrating bureaucratic delays.
Yet, every time she saw a wall being built, a floor slab hoisted into place, saw this street visibly rising from the ruins, a tremendous sense of pride surged in her heart. They were not just building houses; they were rebuilding the soul of a city, redrawing the future skyline for a nation that had suffered greatly.
In the evening, workers left the site in twos and threes. Svetlana stayed behind alone, carefully checking the day's progress against the blueprints. The setting sun's rays bathed the unfinished building frames, casting long shadows. She could almost see the near future, when this street would once again be brightly lit, where people would stroll, shop, and laugh, as if the war had never happened.

options.name: Brick by brick, building not just structures, but hope.

title: Procurement Prices at the Market
desc:
Chernihiv's open-air market was bustling with a long-lost liveliness. The sun shone brightly, and along the muddy paths, stalls displayed a variety of farm produce: freshly dug potatoes, crisp cabbages, homemade pickled cucumbers, and a few live chickens flapping their bound feet. Farmers hawked their wares while bargaining with city dwellers who came to purchase.
Uncle Oleg, an old farmer who had tilled the land his entire life, was in particularly high spirits today. Sacks filled with this year's wheat harvest sat before him. Beside him, a young man in uniform was diligently writing in a notebook. He was a grain procurement officer sent by the new government.
“Comrade Oleg, this batch of wheat is good quality. According to the latest procurement price, the total is… this many rubles.” The young man finished his calculations and handed over a wad of crisp new banknotes.
Oleg took the money, carefully counted it twice, an incredulous smile spreading across his face. “This much? It’s… nearly double what the Germans gave last year!” Last year, the Germans had only been willing to exchange a few nearly worthless 'Occupation Zone Marks' for his grain, at ridiculously low prices, practically daylight robbery. If he hadn't secretly hidden some, he and his family would have starved long ago.
“This is the state’s new policy,” the young man said with a smile. “Reduce the burden on farmers, raise procurement prices, encourage everyone to grow more grain, sell more grain. Life will get better and better.” He also told Oleg that there might be new subsidies for fertilizer and farm tools this autumn.
Oleg was so moved he could barely speak, just nodded repeatedly. He carefully tucked the money into his coat, feeling its weight—not just the weight of banknotes, but the weight of hope for life. Other farmers gathered around, chattering, asking about the new policies, their faces all lit with a similar, long-lost ease and anticipation. The market's clamor seemed even more cheerful.

options.name: The sweat of the black earth finally yields weighty rubles.

title: Train to Kharkiv
desc:
Inside the overcrowded third-class carriage, the air was thick, filled with the smells of sweat, smoke, and cheap food. Nineteen-year-old Natasha tightly clutched a patched old bundle containing all her belongings. Leaning against the window, she watched the familiar Ukrainian countryside scenes flash by—endless fields, scattered villages, solitary poplar trees. This was the place she grew up, but she was leaving it for a distant, unfamiliar big city—Kharkiv.
Most passengers in the carriage were like her, young people heading to the city seeking opportunities. They either excitedly discussed their aspirations for future factory life or stared blankly out the window, their faces tinged with apprehension about the unknown. Recruitment posters plastered the village notice boards: Kharkiv's tractor factory, Dnipropetrovsk's steel mill, Kyiv's construction sites… all summoning young labor. The city offered jobs, higher wages, electric lights, cinemas, and… the future.
Natasha’s parents didn't want her to leave; village life, though poor, was stable. But Natasha didn’t want to spend her whole life tending a few meager acres, repeating the life of her ancestors. She wanted to see the outside world, learn a skill, live… a different life. The radio announced daily that the country needed builders, that cities needed young people.
The train let out a long whistle and began to slow down. Outside the window, low farmhouses gradually gave way to towering chimneys and factory buildings. Kharkiv had arrived. Natasha took a deep breath and squeezed off the train with the crowd. The platform thronged with people, the noise deafening. She felt a little dizzy, but mostly excited. This was the city, full of opportunities, and also full of challenges. She didn’t know if she could gain a foothold here, but she knew she couldn't go back.

options.name: The train speeds ahead, carrying departing footsteps and city dreams.

title: Argument in the Tavern
desc:
In a small tavern by the Dnieper River in Dnipropetrovsk, smoke filled the air and voices buzzed. Several steelworkers, just off their shift, sat around a greasy table, drinking cheap beer, eating black bread and salted fish, loudly arguing about something.
“I say, Vasyl, you’re wrong!” a burly man with a beard slammed his fist on the table. “Why say we Russians coming here are the same as the Germans? We are the liberators who drove them out!”
“Liberators?” Vasyl, sitting opposite him, a middle-aged man with sharp eyes and a Ukrainian accent, sneered. “Yes, drove out the wolf, and in came the bear. Before, it was German soldiers on the streets, now it’s your patrols; before, swastikas on the walls, now it’s similar Russian flags; before, we had to learn German, now we have to learn Russian… What’s different?”
“How is it not different?!” the bearded man flared up. “We brought factories! We brought jobs! We didn’t treat you like slaves like the German devils did! We are all brothers in the great Slavic family!”
“Brothers?” Vasyl raised his glass and drained it. “Some ‘brothers’ don’t quite treat us as their own. My son was punished at school by that teacher from Moscow just for speaking a few words of Ukrainian! In your newspapers, how many articles are about our Ukrainian heroes? Isn’t it always praising yourselves!”
“That… that’s a minority situation!” The bearded man was somewhat at a loss for words. “The policy is good, it’s just that people below implement it wrongly… Besides, let the past be past, isn’t it good for everyone to build a new life together now?”
“The past?” Vasyl’s eyes grew deep and sorrowful. “Some things cannot be forgotten. The Great Famine, the purges, and… the war. This land of ours has shed too much blood, both red and black.”
Silence fell in the tavern, only the faint sound of a distant radio drifting in. Several young men at the next table seemed to have overheard their argument, exchanging complex glances. Rebuilding trust, forging identity, was far more difficult than repairing a bombed-out bridge.

options.name: Scars may heal, but they still ache when touched.

title: Meeting by the Mill
desc:
The old mill at the village entrance had been cleaned up, whitewashed anew, and adorned with a wooden sign reading “’Common Plowing’ Agricultural Production Cooperative.” Inside the mill, a dozen villagers, men and women, young and old, sat around a long wooden table, intensely discussing something. Scattered on the table were several rough blueprints and notebooks filled with numbers.
“I think we should turn that low-lying land into a fish pond first!” said Ivan, the cooperative leader, a shrewd and capable former partisan. “Fish farming yields quick results; we can distribute dividends by the end of the year!”
“No!” someone immediately objected—it was Mikhailo, an experienced old farmer. “That land, though low-lying, has good soil. If we just repair the irrigation ditch, we can grow good vegetables! It’s more reliable than fish farming!”
“How much labor does repairing the ditch require? How much time? By the time it’s done, the day lily buds will have withered!” Ivan slammed the table.
“Fish farming is risky! If disease strikes, not a single one will be left!” Mikhailo retorted stubbornly.
…The debate lasted a long time. Everyone wanted to contribute to the cooperative's development, but their ideas differed. This was a cooperative formed spontaneously by the villagers; the land still belonged to individual families, but tools, livestock, and labor could be shared, with income distributed according to work. It was a new thing, different from the past small-scale farming where everyone fended for themselves, and also different from the state-imposed collective farms. Everyone was exploring, full of enthusiasm, but also full of uncertainty.
Finally, Anna, the most respected old teacher in the village, stepped in to mediate. “Comrades, stop arguing. How about this: we can use the low-lying land to raise ducks first; it requires less investment and yields quick returns. Meanwhile, everyone contributes some labor to slowly repair the irrigation ditch. By next spring, we can plant vegetables. This way, we don't delay either task. How about it?”
Everyone looked at each other, finding this compromise feasible. Thus, the new plan was scribbled crookedly into the notebook. Outside, the setting sun slowly descended, casting a warm, hopeful glow on this newly started cooperative.

options.name: Many hands make light work; the flame may not rise straight, but it always brings warmth.

title: Gifts of the Earth
desc:
Olena knelt on the field ridge, scooped up a handful of loose, damp black earth, and inhaled its scent deeply. It was a unique aroma, a blend of humus, rainwater, and plant roots—the smell of life, the distinctive fragrance of this Ukrainian black soil. For centuries, this land had nourished her ancestors and buried her relatives. It had generously offered golden waves of wheat and silently endured the ravages of war.
Her fingers felt the warmth and power of the soil. Spring had arrived; it was planting season. In the distance, the collective farm's tractors were working, emitting a rhythmic roar. Her husband and son were also busy in the fields, their figures appearing small yet incredibly determined against the vast landscape.
After the war, everything was slowly recovering. Although life remained arduous, and fertilizer and seeds still needed planned distribution, at least the land had returned to the hands of the cultivators, no longer forced to lie fallow or grow alien crops to satisfy the greedy demands of distant empires.
Olena stood up, brushing the dirt from her knees. She took a handful of plump sunflower seeds from a cloth bag and carefully scattered them onto the freshly plowed soil. She knew that with diligent cultivation, this magical black earth would never fail them. It would once again bloom with golden flowers, bear heavy fruit, like a loving mother selflessly nurturing her children.
The wind blew across the fields, carrying the scent of cooking smoke from the distant village. Olena straightened her back, gazing at the boundless fields and the azure sky, her heart filled with peace and an ancient, earth-rooted sense of solidity.

options.name: Beneath the black earth pulses an unceasing life.

title: Oath Before the Blast Furnace
desc:
The massive blast furnace once again spewed fiery molten iron, bathing the entire workshop in an orange glow. Amidst the deafening roar, sweat-drenched workers operated huge mechanical arms, transporting searing steel ingots to the next process. The Azovstal Steel Plant in Mariupol, an industrial behemoth nearly destroyed in the war, was stubbornly regenerating from the ruins.
Andrei, an experienced furnace master, stared intently at the leaping flames in the furnace mouth, judging the temperature by years of experience. His face was blackened by the intense heat, his arms covered in old scars. During the war, he had led workers to continue production under German shelling until being forced to evacuate at the last moment. Now, he was back, back to the place where he had dedicated most of his youth.
Reconstruction was exceptionally difficult. Much equipment was destroyed or removed by the Germans, workshops were reduced to rubble, and skilled colleagues were dead or scattered. They started almost from scratch, clearing debris, repairing machines, reassembling the workforce. But no one complained; everyone held a suppressed determination.
“Master Andrei!” a young apprentice ran over, shouting excitedly. “The first batch of qualified molten steel is out! Tested and approved!”
A smile finally touched Andrei’s tense face. He nodded, pumping his fist vigorously. This wasn't just a batch of molten steel; it was the resurrection call of Azovstal, the hope for Ukraine's heavy industry revival. He could already envision tractors made from their steel racing across fields, new bridges and buildings constructed, weapons forged to defend the homeland.
The end-of-shift whistle blew. Workers, dragging their weary bodies, walked out of the workshop, covered in grease and iron filings, yet their eyes shone with light. Andrei stood before the blast furnace, gazing at the ceaselessly flowing molten iron, silently making an oath in his heart: He must make this factory stronger than before, must ensure Ukrainian steel once again supports the nation's spine.

options.name: The body of steel, reforged in fire.

title: Forest of Chimneys
desc:
From Donetsk to Zaporizhzhia, then to Dnipropetrovsk, across the vast expanse of eastern Ukraine, factory chimneys were rising again like bamboo shoots after rain, forming a unique 'forest of chimneys.' The daytime sky was often shrouded in smoke of various colors, while nights were illuminated by the glare of blast furnaces and coking plants. This was the heartland of Ukrainian heavy industry, the engine of national reconstruction.
In the iron ore mines of Kryvyi Rih, giant excavators tirelessly gnawed at mountains rich in iron ore. At the Kharkiv Tractor Plant, newly assembled tractors lined the factory square, awaiting shipment across the country. On the dam of the Dnieper Hydroelectric Station, engineers nervously repaired generators damaged by the war.
Sergei, a specialist from the Central Planning Bureau responsible for coordinating production plans among factories, sat on a jolting train, traveling through this vibrant industrial zone. His briefcase bulged with reports, charts, and applications. Every factory lacked funds, equipment, skilled workers, raw materials… problems piled up like mountains. But every time he saw the rising factory buildings, the determined yet weary expressions on the workers' faces, the train cars loaded with coal, ore, and steel, a strong sense of mission surged within him.
They were building a powerful industrial base, one capable of supporting national security, improving people's lives, and realizing the dream of modernization. This process might be accompanied by pollution, inefficiency, and various problems, but the overall direction was clear, the forward march resolute. As the train passed a large chemical plant belching thick smoke, Sergei opened the window and took a deep breath of the air, pungent with chemical odors. This, he thought, was the smell of progress.

options.name: Machines roar, Ukraine's heart beats anew.

title: Order to Initiate Reconstruction Work in the Caucasus Region
desc:
To: Responsible Comrades, Caucasus Special Administrative Region (Provisional) Reconstruction Steering Group
From: Makarov, Fifth Office, Southern Bureau, Central Restoration and Development Committee
Subject: Order to Immediately Initiate the First Phase of Restoration and Reconstruction Work in the Caucasus Region
To all Comrades of the Steering Group:
Given that the Caucasus region has been liberated from fascist bandits and their vassals, according to unified directives from the Central Committee, it is hereby ordered that the first phase of restoration and reconstruction work in the region begin immediately. The Caucasus region holds a unique geographical position, possesses a complex ethnic composition, and has long suffered from brutal rule and war devastation. The reconstruction task is extremely arduous and profoundly significant. Current core tasks include: One, rapidly conduct a thorough assessment of the damage to the Baku oil fields, Georgian manganese mines, and major transportation routes (especially the Trans-Caucasian Highway and Railway), submit a report, and clarify repair priorities. Two, inventory regional agricultural potential, register land and livestock conditions, and immediately begin preparations to restore subtropical crop cultivation and mountain animal husbandry. Three, organize forces to repair or rebuild basic livelihood facilities in key cities (such as Tbilisi, Baku, Sochi), ensure basic supplies, and stabilize public sentiment. Four, resolutely eliminate remaining hostile armed elements (including but not limited to partisans, former collaborator forces), maintain social order, and strictly prevent sabotage activities. Five, in carrying out the work, pay close attention to the complex local historical legacy issues and ethnic sentiments, and cautiously advance various policies. The Central Committee understands the difficulties involved; subsequent resources will be gradually coordinated. Act immediately, without delay!

options.name: The snow mountains bear witness; we vow to rejuvenate this land.

title: Echoes in the Valley
desc:
The mules of the geological survey team struggled up the rugged mountain path, their hoofbeats echoing in the vast valley. Artyom, a young geologist from Moscow, wrestled with a crumpled topographical map and a compass, sweat soaking his hairline. Beside him walked his taciturn local guide, an old Georgian named Giorgi, who watched Artyom's clumsy efforts with a faint, almost imperceptible smile mingling pity and mockery.
“Young man, did the map not tell you that stones also speak?” Giorgi finally broke the silence, his voice as clear as a mountain stream. “Following the sheep’s path is usually more reliable than following the path drawn in ink.”
Artyom flushed slightly, lowering the map. “Uncle Giorgi, the report says this area has rich manganese and copper deposits, vital for the country's reconstruction. We must find the precise location of the veins.”
The old man said no more, merely pointing towards a distant rock face of a slightly darker hue. “My grandfather’s grandfather dug stones from that area, for the Tsar’s cannonballs. Later, for Bukharin’s tanks. And later still… for the Germans’ airplanes.” He sighed. “The mountain stones don’t recognize flags; they only recognize the hands that dig them. You came, so they serve you. When you leave…”
Artyom followed the old man’s pointing finger. The rock face glowed with a metallic sheen in the setting sun. This magnificent and ancient mountain range generously held the lifeblood of industry, yet it had also impassively witnessed the coming and going of too many conquerors. They were here to take, in the name of the state and the plan, for that grand 'reconstruction' goal. But these mountains, these stones, seemed to have their own unyielding rhythm.

options.name: Wealth lies hidden deep, awaiting the digging hand, regardless of its origin.

title: Wind off the Caspian
desc:
Baku, the wind always carries a thick, oily smell that even the breeze from the Caspian Sea cannot fully dissipate. Derelict old drilling rigs from the 'Nobel Brothers' era stood like rusted skeletons along the shore, forming a strange contrast with the newly repaired, smoke-belching new derricks nearby.
Engineer Leonid Sokolov, an experienced petroleum expert, stood beside a huge, pitted oil storage tank, gesturing to a group of local Azerbaijani workers, trying to explain a new valve installation plan. His Russian was peppered with a few stiff Azerbaijani words, while the workers watched him with eyes mixing curiosity, skepticism, and weariness.
“This new pressure valve, it’s the latest model allocated from… above!” Sokolov strained to make his voice heard over the noise of the derrick repairs nearby. “Installing it will increase efficiency, and also… make things safer!”
An old worker, his face smeared with oil, wearing a headscarf, asked in a thick accent: “Safe? When the Germans occupied, nobody cared if we were safe; the wells caught fire every few days. Now you’re here. The oil is the same oil, but our lives… are they still our lives?”
Sokolov was momentarily speechless. He knew war and occupation had left deep scars and distrust among the people here. Rebuilding the oil fields wasn’t just about repairing machines and pipelines; it was also about mending hearts. He pointed to the derricks working in the distance: “Old man, look, we are trying to make everything better. The country needs oil, just like a person needs blood. You have experience, we have technology (though much of it is newly learned too). Let’s work together. Baku’s oil will flow again, and life will get better too.”
The old worker looked at him silently, then slowly nodded. Perhaps he believed his words, or perhaps simply because, other than working, they had no other choice. The Caspian wind blew past, carrying more roaring sounds of restarting machinery from deep within the oil fields.

options.name: Can black gold wash away red memories?

title: Sanatorium Vouchers by the Sea
desc:
On the beaches of Sochi, a scattering of people appeared, dressed in various swimsuits (mostly old-style Soviet one-piece suits or homemade beach shorts). They cautiously dipped their feet into the cool Black Sea water, uttering cries of surprise or complaint. In the distance, several formerly luxurious, now slightly dilapidated sanatoriums were undergoing exterior painting and repairs.

Margarita, a waitress working in a local state-run restaurant, was somewhat impatiently serving a table of a 'sanatorium delegation' from Siberia. Most were miners or factory labor models, here on state-awarded sanatorium vouchers, curious about everything, yet also carrying a simple reserve. They always chose the cheapest dishes when ordering, and even hesitated to share a bottle of kvass amongst themselves.

“Comrade, another bottle of kvass!” shouted a loud-voiced miner. Margarita acknowledged and turned to fetch it. She remembered during the German occupation, this place was also filled with 'recuperating' people, but they were impeccably uniformed, arrogant German officers and their mistresses. They spent lavishly and lorded over the locals.

The people arriving now were different; they were 'one of us,' the 'working people.' Yet Margarita always felt a distance. They came from the remote Russian heartland, spoke with accents she wasn't used to, marveled at the Black Sea's palm trees and warm climate. While she and her family had endured too much turmoil and hardship on this beautiful land, always somewhat skeptical of the 'sunshine, beaches, workers' paradise' depicted in propaganda posters.

Outside the restaurant window, several children chased the waves. The sun was bright, the sea blue. Perhaps, letting people from different places come here to see the sea, relax a bit, was a good thing in itself. At least, it was much better than hearing cannons.

options.name: The waves of the Black Sea wash upon the sands of different eras.

title: Dots on the Map
desc:
The geological survey report lay spread out on the table in the temporary headquarters in Grozny, marked with dense symbols and lines in different colored pencils. An official with thinning hair peered through a magnifying glass at several red dots marked on the map near the Chechen mountains.
“So, Comrade Petrenko, are you certain these marks represent… oil?” He looked up, asking the weary-eyed geology team leader beside him, who wore mud-caked survey gear.
“Reasonably certain, Comrade Director,” Petrenko rubbed his eyes. “Based on our preliminary drilling samples and geological analysis, this area contains significant underground oil and gas reserves. The volume could be… quite substantial.”
The official’s eyes lit up. “Substantial? Excellent! Excellent! This means we’ve found a new energy base besides Baku! This is a huge boost for the reconstruction of the Caucasus and the entire country!” He rubbed his hands excitedly. “We must immediately organize forces, intensify exploration, and formulate an extraction plan as soon as possible!”
Petrenko hesitated for a moment. “Comrade Director, the situation might be… somewhat complex. These areas are mountainous, rugged terrain, with difficult access. Moreover… the local inhabitants, mainly Chechens, they seem… unwelcoming towards our exploration activities. Some team members reported hearing gunshots at night, and some equipment was inexplicably damaged.”
The official’s excitement instantly faded, replaced by a gloomy expression. “Unwelcoming? Humph, this is our country’s land; the underground wealth belongs to all the people! What right do they have to be unwelcoming?” He rapped the table. “Comrade Petrenko, your task is to find oil, not handle local relations! Security issues will naturally be handled by comrades responsible for security. You just need to tell me, can the oil be extracted!”
Petrenko looked at the bright red dots on the map, seeming to see the black oil that might gush forth in the future, and also sensing the unpredictable conflicts and troubles that would inevitably follow.

options.name: Underground wealth often comes hand-in-hand with surface strife.

title: Trucks Towards the Mountains
desc:
A convoy of dusty trucks moved slowly along the winding mountain roads, their beds crammed with immigrant families from central Russia. They carried all their possessions—tightly bound bedding rolls, creaking old wooden chests, and a few chickens stuffed into cages. Children's faces pressed against the gaps in the truck's sideboards, curiously and timidly gazing at the unfamiliar, rolling Caucasus mountains outside.
Valentina held her young son tightly, her heart filled with both anticipation and anxiety about the future. Government propagandists had depicted the Caucasus as a sunny, fertile land awaiting settlers to cultivate. They said there was fertile land to be distributed, new factories needing workers, and the state provided resettlement subsidies. For them, who scraped a living from the soil back in Ryazan and saved barely a few rubles year-round, this seemed like a godsend.
However, when the trucks rolled into a somewhat dilapidated Dagestani village, they weren't greeted by the enthusiastic scenes depicted in the posters. Some local villagers in traditional clothing stood by the roadside, eyeing these 'outsiders' with a scrutinizing, less than friendly gaze. The air was filled with the smell of unfamiliar language and food. The village houses were mostly low and old, far from the 'modernized new countryside' described in the propaganda.
The official in charge of resettlement, a Russian cadre who also looked somewhat weary, led them to a row of newly erected, rather basic wooden plank houses. “Comrades, you’ll stay here for now,” he said, pointing at the houses. “Land and job placements are being coordinated and will be arranged soon. Everyone must foster unity with the local comrades, help each other, and jointly build our great homeland!”
Valentina looked at the unfamiliar mountains, unfamiliar people, unfamiliar houses, her heart filled with panic. Was this truly the new homeland they dreamed of? Could they put down roots here? She didn't know. She only knew they couldn't go back.

options.name: The new homeland: a promise, and an unknown migration.

title: Whispers in the Market
desc:
Tbilisi market: noisy, crowded, filled with the mixed scents of various spices, grilled meat, and cheap tobacco.
